paragraphs: An earthquake struck off Crete on 21 July 365 CE, generating a tsunami that hit the coasts of Crete, Libya, Egypt and Cyprus. In Alexandria, the historian Ammianus Marcellinus described the sea withdrawing from the shore before returning as a wall of water that carried ships onto rooftops and drowned people who had gone out to gather stranded fish.

Modern seismologists estimate the earthquake's magnitude at around 8, generated by a rupture along the Hellenic subduction zone south of Crete. The date is still marked in Alexandria's Christian calendar centuries later, and the associated uplift of Crete's western coastline is measurable in raised marine terraces studied by geologists today.

Colliery spoil had been tipped for decades on a hillside above the Welsh village of Aberfan, on a slope known to sit over underground springs. On the morning of 21 October 1966, after heavy rain, roughly 150,000 cubic metres of waterlogged waste broke loose and slid downhill into Pantglas Junior School.

The slide killed 144 people, 116 of them children who had just settled into their classrooms for the day. A tribunal found the National Coal Board had known of the risk and failed to act; no one was prosecuted, and the Board took years, and disputed compensation from bereaved families, before fully repaying the disaster fund it had drained to help pay for removing the remaining tips.

On 5 June 1981, the CDC's Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report described five previously healthy gay men in Los Angeles who had developed a rare pneumonia, Pneumocystis carinii, usually seen only in patients with severely damaged immune systems. Two had already died by the time the report went out.

Doctors had no name yet for what was killing them; early press coverage called it gay-related immune deficiency before the term AIDS was adopted in 1982. The virus behind it, HIV, was not isolated until 1983. Within a decade the disease had spread to every continent, and the five cases in that first report are now read as the epidemic's earliest documented trace.

On Good Friday, 27 March 1964, a rupture along the Aleutian megathrust near Prince William Sound produced a magnitude 9.2 earthquake, the strongest ever recorded in North America and the second strongest anywhere. Shaking in Anchorage lasted about four to five minutes, long enough to level buildings that had ridden out shorter quakes before.

The quake and its tsunamis killed around 131 to 143 people, most drowned by waves that struck coastal Alaska within minutes and reached California and Hawaii within hours. Much of Alaska's coastline shifted vertically by several metres, and the town of Valdez was relocated to firmer ground after the shoreline it sat on liquefied and slid into the sea.

An earthquake struck the region around Aleppo, in modern Syria, on 11 October 1138, toppling the citadel and much of the surrounding city and countryside. It came during a period when Aleppo was contested between Crusader states and Muslim rulers, and the destruction of fortifications shaped the military balance in the region for years afterward.

A widely repeated figure of 230,000 dead comes from a fifteenth century Egyptian chronicler, Ibn Taghribirdi, writing centuries after the event. Modern seismologists think that number likely combines this earthquake with separate ones nearby in 1137 and 1139, and while Aleppo is still ranked among history's deadliest recorded earthquakes, the true toll is unknown.

The Andrea Doria, an Italian ocean liner en route to New York, collided with the Swedish liner Stockholm in dense fog off Nantucket on the night of 25 July 1956. Both ships had radar, but their crews misread each other's course and closed rather than turned away, and the Stockholm's reinforced ice-breaking bow tore deep into the Andrea Doria's side.

The Andrea Doria stayed afloat for eleven hours before sinking, long enough for nearby ships, alerted by radio, to rescue most of the roughly 1,660 people aboard. Forty six died, most in the initial collision. The wreck settled on its side in about 240 feet of water and remains a popular, and dangerous, scuba diving site.

The Ansei earthquakes were a cluster of major quakes that struck Japan across 1854 and 1855, named for the Ansei era in which they fell. The last and most destructive, on 11 November 1855, was centred directly beneath Edo, the shogunal capital that is now Tokyo, and struck at ten at night when most residents were indoors with open cooking fires and lamps lit.

Estimates for deaths in Edo range from about 7,000 to 10,000, drawn from contemporary temple and neighbourhood records rather than any single government count, and roughly 14,000 buildings were destroyed across the city. Woodblock prints depicting a giant catfish thrashing beneath Japan, blamed in folklore for causing earthquakes, were sold in large numbers in Edo in the weeks after.

An earthquake struck Antioch, then one of the Byzantine Empire's largest cities, in late May 526 CE, during morning hours when the streets were full of visitors for the feast of the Ascension. Fires broke out among the collapsed buildings and burned for days afterward, adding to the destruction from the initial shock and its aftershocks.

Contemporary chroniclers put the dead at around 250,000, a figure historians treat as an estimate rather than a count, since no census existed to check it against. The Byzantine emperor Justin I sent money for rebuilding, but the city was struck again by a further severe earthquake in 528, before it had fully recovered.

Roman troops returning from campaigns in the east brought a new disease into the empire around 165 CE, and it spread along military and trade roads for roughly fifteen years. The physician Galen described its symptoms, including fever, vomiting and a skin rash, which has led modern researchers to suspect smallpox, though the diagnosis is not certain.

Estimates of the dead range from a few million to as many as ten million across the empire, figures reconstructed from Roman records of troop shortages and depopulated towns rather than any contemporary head count. The emperor Marcus Aurelius's co ruler, Lucius Verus, is generally reported to have died of it in 169 CE.

A magnitude 6.8 earthquake struck northern Armenia on 7 December 1988, centred near the city of Spitak, which was almost entirely destroyed. Leninakan, Armenia's second-largest city, and the town of Kirovakan were also badly damaged, largely because Soviet-era apartment blocks had been built with substandard concrete and inadequate reinforcement.

Official Soviet figures put the dead at around 25,000, though Armenian estimates run higher, and roughly half a million people were left homeless in freezing winter conditions. The disaster prompted the Soviet Union to accept international aid for the first time since the Second World War, including teams and supplies from the United States.

An earthquake of roughly magnitude 7.3 struck the Turkmen city of Ashgabat before dawn on 6 October 1948, destroying most of its buildings while residents slept. Soviet authorities classified the disaster and barred foreign observers, and for four decades official Soviet publications gave a death toll of about 10,000.

Later Turkmen government figures, released after independence, put the toll far higher, around 110,000 to 176,000, closer to two thirds of the city's population at the time. The wide gap between the Soviet-era figure and later estimates reflects deliberate concealment rather than uncertain counting, since the state suppressed even the fact that a quake had occurred.

The crisis began on 2 July 1997, when Thailand abandoned its currency peg to the dollar after months of speculative attacks it could no longer afford to fight. The baht collapsed, and the panic spread through Indonesia, South Korea, Malaysia and the Philippines within weeks as foreign investors pulled capital out of economies that had borrowed heavily in dollars.

Currencies lost half their value or more, stock markets crashed and Indonesia's Suharto government fell in the unrest that followed in 1998. The IMF extended over 100 billion dollars in bailouts tied to austerity conditions that many economists later judged had deepened the recessions they were meant to cure.

The virus was first identified in Guizhou, China, in February 1957 and reached Singapore, Hong Kong and the United States within months, carried by ships and commercial air travel faster than any earlier flu strain had moved. It was an H2N2 strain, new enough that almost no one had prior immunity, and it spread through schools and army barracks before health authorities had a name for it.

Estimates of the global death toll run from about one to two million, compiled later from national health records that varied widely in how carefully influenza deaths were counted at the time. A vaccine reached the United States by August 1957, produced quickly because researchers had been tracking the new strain since its identification in Asia that spring, but too late to stop the first wave.

Australia's 2019-2020 fire season, later called Black Summer, burned across more than 18 million hectares after a record drought and a run of extreme heat, sending smoke as far as New Zealand and South America. Thirty-three people died directly in the fires, and over 3,000 homes were destroyed.

A WWF-commissioned study estimated that nearly three billion animals were killed or displaced, including 143 million mammals and over 2 billion reptiles, a figure well above earlier estimates released while the fires were still burning. Several threatened species lost large portions of their remaining habitat in a single season.

In 586 BCE, after a prolonged siege following a rebellion by King Zedekiah, Babylonian forces under Nebuchadnezzar II breached Jerusalem's walls. Soldiers burned the royal palace and the First Temple, built centuries earlier under Solomon, and tore down the city's fortifications so it could not be defended again.

Much of the surviving population, including craftsmen, priests and the royal court, was deported to Babylon, beginning the period Jewish tradition calls the Babylonian Exile. It ended the independent Kingdom of Judah, and the exile that followed reshaped Jewish religious practice around texts and communal memory rather than a temple that no longer stood.

A cyclone with winds near 250 kilometres an hour struck Bangladesh's Chittagong coast on the night of 29 April 1991, pushing a storm surge of up to six metres over low-lying islands and coastal farmland where warnings had reached many residents too late to act. Offshore islands such as Sandwip and Kutubdia were among the hardest hit.

Estimates of the dead run to around 138,000, with the storm surge, rather than the wind, responsible for most deaths as people were swept from their homes with nowhere higher to go. The scale of the loss pushed Bangladesh to build thousands of raised concrete cyclone shelters, credited with sharply reducing deaths in later storms.

Severe flooding in 1974 destroyed much of that year's rice crop in Bangladesh, only three years after its war of independence had already wrecked transport and administration needed to move food where it was needed. Rice prices rose sharply through the year as traders hoarded stock, pushing food out of reach of landless labourers well before any physical shortage became acute.

Deaths are estimated at up to 1.5 million, concentrated among agricultural labourers who had no land to fall back on and no wages once the flooded fields stopped needing workers. The economist Amartya Sen later used the famine as a central case for his argument that famines are driven less by a shortage of food overall than by who can no longer afford to buy it.

Typhoon Nina stalled over Henan province in August 1975 and dropped roughly a year's worth of rain in three days, overwhelming a network of dams built for a much smaller design flood. The Banqiao dam and dozens of smaller dams downstream failed in sequence, sending a wall of water estimated at up to ten kilometres wide across the plain below.

China's official count puts direct flood deaths at around 26,000, but that figure excludes the famine and disease that followed in the flood's wake; independent estimates that include those deaths run as high as 240,000. The disaster was kept out of Chinese state records for decades and only became widely known outside China after documents surfaced in the 1990s.

On 4 August 2020, a fire in a Beirut port warehouse ignited 2,750 tonnes of ammonium nitrate that had sat there, poorly stored, since being unloaded from the cargo ship Rhosus in 2014. The blast was felt in Cyprus, over 200 kilometres away, and levelled much of the port and the neighbourhoods around it.

Lebanese authorities recorded at least 218 deaths and roughly 7,000 injuries, with about 300,000 people left without habitable homes. No senior official was convicted in the years afterwards despite repeated investigations, and the explosion deepened an economic collapse that had already emptied Lebanese bank accounts of their value that same year.

The famine of 1943 struck Bengal after cyclone damage, a fungal disease that ruined much of the rice crop, and the loss of Burmese rice imports following Japan's occupation of Burma. Colonial authorities diverted grain and boats toward the war effort and denied entry permits for outside relief, while Winston Churchill's wartime cabinet resisted requests to divert shipping to feed the province.

Estimates of the dead range from 1.5 million to three million, figures reconstructed later from famine commission reports and demographic surveys rather than any contemporaneous count. Most deaths came from disease among the weakened rather than starvation alone, as cholera and malaria spread through refugees who had left the countryside for Calcutta.

The cyclone made landfall on the night of 12 to 13 November 1970 on the low-lying islands of the Ganges delta, then part of East Pakistan, pushing a storm surge of several metres over land that sat barely above sea level and had no cyclone shelters. Warnings were issued but reached few of the farming and fishing communities on the offshore islands in time.

Estimates of the dead range from 300,000 to 500,000, gathered afterward from surviving relatives and local officials rather than any single census, since entire villages were washed away with no one left to report them missing. The disaster's slow, uneven federal response fed grievances in East Pakistan that fed directly into the war for Bangladeshi independence the following year.

On the night of 2 to 3 December 1984, water entered a storage tank of methyl isocyanate at a Union Carbide pesticide plant in Bhopal, India, triggering a runaway reaction that vented a dense toxic cloud over the sleeping city. Safety systems that might have contained it, including a refrigeration unit and a gas scrubber, were shut down or undersized.

The Madhya Pradesh government later confirmed 3,787 immediate deaths, while independent estimates of total deaths, including those from long-term exposure, run as high as 25,000. Union Carbide paid 470 million dollars in a 1989 settlement, its former chairman Warren Anderson was charged in India but never extradited, and the site remains contaminated.

After the Igbo-led south-east of Nigeria declared independence as Biafra in 1967, the federal government imposed a blockade on food, medicine and fuel entering the breakaway region, treating starvation as a tool of the war rather than a side effect of it. Aid flights that tried to reach Biafran territory faced federal naval and air blockade for most of the conflict.

Images of starving children, marked by the swollen bellies of kwashiorkor, brought the famine into newspapers and television worldwide and helped establish humanitarian organisations that still operate today, including the group that became Doctors Without Borders. Estimates of the dead range from 500,000 to two million, most from starvation and disease rather than combat, before the war ended with Biafra's surrender in January 1970.

Genoese ships fleeing a Mongol siege of the Black Sea port of Caffa docked in Messina, Sicily, in October 1347 carrying sailors already dying. From there the disease moved up through Italy and into France, Spain and England within two years, spreading fastest along trade routes and rivers, since ports and market towns exposed the most people to the fleas and rats that carried it.

Contemporaries called it the Great Mortality; the name Black Death was applied centuries later. Modern estimates put its toll across Europe at around a third of the population over the following years, though in some cities, such as Florence, more than half the residents are thought to have died, based on tax and burial records rather than any contemporary head count.

By 1349 the plague that had landed in Sicily two years earlier had spread across nearly all of Europe, and this was its worst single year in most of the cities it reached. Grave diggers in London and Paris could not keep pace with the dead, and mass burial pits, some holding hundreds of bodies layered without individual graves, have been excavated at sites including London's East Smithfield.

No city kept a reliable count, so historians rely on tax rolls, manorial records and church burial registers that show sudden, sharp population drops in this year specifically. Entire villages recorded in earlier surveys disappear from the record after 1349, and it took some regions of Europe more than a century to recover their pre-plague population.

The Black Sea deluge hypothesis holds that around 5600 BCE, rising water from the Mediterranean broke through the Bosphorus and poured into what had been a smaller freshwater lake, raising its level rapidly and flooding surrounding lowlands. Marine geologists first proposed the idea after finding drowned shorelines and freshwater mollusc shells beneath the sea's saltwater layers.

The theory has been linked, speculatively, to flood traditions in the region, including the Mesopotamian and biblical flood stories, though most scholars treat that connection as unproven. Later studies have questioned how sudden the flooding actually was, with some geologists arguing the sea rose over centuries rather than in one abrupt event.

A 50-foot steel tank holding 2.3 million gallons of molasses burst on Commercial Street in Boston's North End on 15 January 1919, sending a wave estimated at 25 feet high through the streets. The tank had been filled to capacity days earlier without adequate testing, after previous leaks had simply been painted over.

Twenty-one people died, most suffocated by the syrup rather than drowned outright, and about 150 more were injured. A subsequent class-action lawsuit, unusual for the time, found the United States Industrial Alcohol Company responsible and pushed Boston toward requiring engineers to certify new construction.

Between roughly 1200 and 1150 BCE, the Hittite Empire, Mycenaean Greece and several other eastern Mediterranean states broke down within a few generations. Trade networks that had carried tin, copper and grain across the region collapsed with them, and cities including Ugarit and Mycenae were destroyed or abandoned.

No single cause explains it. Egyptian records blame raiders they called the Sea Peoples, but drought, earthquakes clustered in a short period, and internal unrest are also documented in the same decades. Writing itself was lost in Greece for centuries afterward, and archaeologists still argue over which of these pressures came first.

Five major earthquakes struck the Calabria region of the Kingdom of Naples between 5 February and 28 March 1783, each estimated at magnitude 5.9 or higher. The first two generated tsunamis that struck the coast; at Scilla, floodwater surged some 200 metres inland and killed more than 1,500 people who had gathered on the shore after fleeing their houses.

Modern estimates put the total dead between 32,000 and 50,000 across the region, a range reflecting incomplete parish and government records from towns that were themselves destroyed. The disaster prompted one of the first scientific field surveys of an earthquake, commissioned by the Bourbon government, which sent investigators to map the damage town by town.

The Camp Fire started on 8 November 2018 from a worn hook on a century-old electrical transmission line owned by Pacific Gas and Electric, in dry hills above Butte County, California. Wind pushed it into the town of Paradise within hours, faster than evacuation routes, built for a much smaller population, could clear.

85 people died and nearly 19,000 structures burned, including about 11,000 homes, making it California's deadliest and most destructive wildfire on record. PG&E later pleaded guilty to 84 counts of involuntary manslaughter over its equipment's role in starting the fire, and paid billions of dollars in settlements to survivors.

On 1 September 1859, the astronomer Richard Carrington watched a bright flare erupt on the sun's surface through a telescope, the first solar flare ever observed by a human eye. A coronal mass ejection following it reached Earth in under 18 hours, far faster than usual, and slammed into the planet's magnetic field.

The resulting geomagnetic storm set telegraph offices on fire in some locations and let operators in North America and Europe send messages with their batteries disconnected, powered by the induced current alone. Aurorae were reported as far south as the Caribbean. It remains the largest recorded geomagnetic storm, and researchers study it as a benchmark for how a repeat event would affect modern power grids and satellites.

An earthquake struck the Pacific coast of North America on the night of 26 January 1700, generated by the Cascadia subduction zone offshore from what is now Washington, Oregon and northern California. There is no written record of the quake in North America, since the region's Indigenous nations kept oral rather than documentary histories, but their oral traditions describe a great shaking and a wave that followed it.

Japanese records fill the gap: coastal towns logged an unexplained orphan tsunami that arrived with no local earthquake to account for it, and the travel time across the Pacific matched a Cascadia rupture to the hour. Tree-ring dating of drowned coastal forests, killed by the sudden land subsidence, confirmed the same date independently, letting geologists pin the magnitude at roughly 8.7 to 9.2.

A drought that began in 1780 failed the monsoon across northern and central India for several consecutive years, and by 1783 wells, tanks and rivers across a wide belt of the subcontinent had run dry. Grain prices rose beyond what most labourers could pay, and starvation was followed by cholera and other disease outbreaks that killed people already weakened by hunger.

Estimates for the dead run from about 11 million to as high as 20 million, a range historians give because no colonial or princely administration kept a systematic count across the affected states. The Chalisa followed a smaller famine in the south the year before, and together the two are thought to have permanently depopulated parts of Rajasthan, Delhi and the Gangetic plain.

The Space Shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch on 28 January 1986, when a rubber O-ring seal in its right solid rocket booster failed in unusually cold Florida weather, letting hot gas burn through and rupture the external fuel tank. All seven crew died, among them Christa McAuliffe, a schoolteacher chosen to be the first ordinary citizen in space, and the launch was carried live into classrooms across the country.

Engineer Roger Boisjoli had warned managers the night before that the O-rings could fail below a certain temperature, and the launch went ahead regardless. The Rogers Commission that investigated grounded the shuttle programme for 32 months and forced NASA to rebuild its internal safety reporting.

A safety test at Chernobyl's Reactor 4 in northern Ukraine went wrong in the early hours of 26 April 1986, when operators disabled key safety systems and a power surge caused steam explosions that blew the reactor's roof off and exposed its core. The resulting fire burned for days, sending radioactive fallout across much of Europe.

Two plant workers died in the explosion, and 28 more died of acute radiation sickness within weeks; the wider death toll from cancers linked to the fallout is still disputed, with estimates ranging from the low thousands to tens of thousands. The nearby city of Pripyat was evacuated within 36 hours and remains abandoned inside a 30-kilometre exclusion zone.

An earthquake struck central Chile on 8 July 1730, centred offshore near Valparaiso and estimated at around magnitude 8.7, one of the largest to hit the region in the colonial era. Spanish accounts describe the ground shaking for several minutes and towns from Concepcion to Valparaiso left largely in ruins.

The quake generated a tsunami that struck the Chilean coast within minutes and, having crossed the Pacific, was recorded reaching Japan hours later, damage that colonial-era records trace over more than 1,000 kilometres of coastline. Because it struck a sparsely documented colonial frontier, most of what is known comes from later reconstructions of shaking intensity and shoreline change rather than a contemporary death count.

Heavy spring snowmelt combined with nine cyclones over the Yangtze basin in the summer of 1931, breaching dykes that had held the river back for generations. Water covered an area larger than England, submerging farmland across Hubei, Anhui and Jiangsu provinces for months rather than days.

Direct drowning killed a comparatively small share of the dead; most died afterward from the famine and disease that followed the flood, as stored grain rotted and cholera spread through refugee camps. Chinese government tallies and later foreign relief estimates range from about two million to as many as four million deaths, the wide gap reflecting how little of the rural toll was ever formally recorded.

A cholera outbreak killed more than 600 people around Broad Street in London's Soho district within about ten days in late August and September 1854, at a time when most doctors still believed the disease spread through foul air rather than contaminated water. John Snow, a local physician, plotted the deaths house by house and found they clustered tightly around a single public water pump.

Snow persuaded local officials to remove the pump handle, after which new cases fell, though the outbreak was already subsiding by then for other reasons. His map and case-by-case interviewing became a founding method of epidemiology, and later investigation traced the contamination to a leaking cesspit near the pump's well, close to a house where an infant with cholera had been nursed.

The magnitude 6.3 earthquake that struck Christchurch on 22 February 2011 was an aftershock of a larger, less destructive quake five months earlier, but its epicentre lay directly beneath the city and the shaking was unusually violent for its size. The central business district, already weakened, took the worst of the damage.

185 people died, most of them in the collapse of a single six-storey office block, the CTV building, which was later found to have been poorly designed for its site. Large parts of central Christchurch were demolished rather than repaired, and rebuilding the city centre took most of the following decade.

On 20 April 1999, two students at Columbine High School in Littleton, Colorado, entered the school with guns and homemade bombs, most of which failed to detonate. They killed 12 students and one teacher and wounded more than 20 others before killing themselves in the library as police waited outside for a tactical team to assemble.

The response drew lasting criticism because officers held a perimeter rather than entering immediately, a decision that reshaped active-shooter protocol for police departments nationwide toward immediate entry. Columbine became the reference point for the string of American school shootings that followed it, and investigators found the attackers had planned it for over a year.

Air France Flight 4590 was taking off from Charles de Gaulle Airport for New York on 25 July 2000 when it ran over a titanium strip shed by another jet on the runway. The debris burst a tyre, and rubber fragments ruptured a fuel tank, igniting a fire that crippled the engines seconds after the Concorde left the ground.

It crashed into a hotel in the town of Gonesse less than two minutes later, killing all 109 people on board and 4 more on the ground, 113 in total. A French court later convicted Continental Airlines, whose plane had dropped the strip, of involuntary manslaughter, though the verdict was overturned on appeal in 2012. Concorde never flew commercially again after 2003.

More than 100 heads of state gathered in Copenhagen in December 2009 for the UN's fifteenth climate conference, aiming to agree binding targets to succeed the Kyoto Protocol. Negotiations ran past their deadline into an overnight session, and a small group of leaders, including US President Barack Obama, drafted a compromise text outside the formal process.

The resulting Copenhagen Accord set a goal of limiting warming to two degrees Celsius but carried no binding emissions targets and was only noted, not adopted, by the full conference after opposition from several developing nations. It was widely reported as a failure at the time, and firmer, though still voluntary, national commitments did not arrive until the Paris Agreement six years later.

The Costa Concordia struck a rock formation off the Tuscan island of Giglio on 13 January 2012 after its captain, Francesco Schettino, sailed close to shore in an unofficial salute to residents. The impact tore a gash in the hull, and the ship rolled onto its side in shallow water within hours as it took on water.

Thirty-two of the roughly 4,200 people aboard died, several of them during a chaotic and delayed evacuation. Schettino left the ship before all passengers were off and was later convicted of manslaughter and abandoning ship, receiving a sixteen-year prison sentence. The wreck was not fully removed from Giglio until 2014.

A coal dust explosion tore through the Courrieres mining complex in northern France on 10 March 1906, the worst mining disaster in European history. Many of the dead were boys as young as twelve, employed underground alongside their fathers.

Rescue teams, some sent from Germany, gave up the search after three weeks; twenty miners who had sealed themselves into a gallery with air and water walked out alive after twenty days. The confirmed death toll was 1,099, and the disaster helped trigger a national miners' strike that spring.

A cluster of unexplained pneumonia cases in Wuhan, China, in December 2019 was traced to a novel coronavirus. The World Health Organisation declared a pandemic on 11 March 2020, and within weeks entire countries had ordered their populations to stay home, closing schools, borders and workplaces on a scale with no precedent in living memory.

Estimates of the toll vary by method: official reports counted around seven million deaths, while the WHO's excess mortality analysis put the figure closer to fifteen million by the end of 2021, accounting for deaths never formally attributed to the virus. Vaccines built on mRNA technology, developed and approved within a year, were credited with sharply cutting deaths once distributed widely.

Nargis made landfall in Myanmar's low-lying Irrawaddy Delta on 2 May 2008, pushing a storm surge more than ten miles inland across a region with almost no high ground to escape to. Entire villages built of wood and thatch were washed away in a single night.

Myanmar's ruling military junta put the toll near 138,000 dead or missing, and initially blocked most foreign aid workers and supplies from entering the country for weeks, a delay humanitarian groups said cost additional lives. International pressure eventually forced the junta to allow a limited relief effort, administered jointly with ASEAN, though independent verification of the final toll remained difficult given restricted access.

An earthquake struck the city of Damghan in northern Iran on 22 December 856 CE, an area then part of the Abbasid Caliphate along a major trade route beneath the Alborz mountains. Medieval Persian chronicles record widespread destruction across the wider Qumis region, not Damghan alone, with entire settlements said to have been levelled.

Modern estimates for the death toll run as high as 200,000, a figure the United States Geological Survey lists among history's deadliest earthquakes, though seismologists caution that medieval chroniclers likely combined casualties from several settlements and possibly separate quakes. More conservative modern readings put the true toll closer to tens of thousands.

In July 1518 a woman named Frau Troffea began dancing in a Strasbourg street and did not stop. Within a week dozens had joined her, and within a month the number was said to have reached several hundred, dancing through exhaustion and bleeding feet. City physicians ruled out demonic possession and diagnosed overheated blood, so the council hired musicians and built a stage, on the theory that dancing it out would cure it.

Accounts of the death toll vary widely, from a few dozen to several hundred, and no contemporary record settled on one figure. The authorities eventually banned music and dancing outright and sent sufferers to a shrine to Saint Vitus, whose name is still attached to the unrelated nervous disorder Sydenham's chorea, itself sometimes called Saint Vitus' dance.

The Deepwater Horizon rig, drilling for BP in the Gulf of Mexico, exploded on 20 April 2010 after a build-up of methane gas, killing eleven crew members and sinking the rig two days later. The wellhead it left behind, a mile beneath the surface, kept releasing crude for 87 days before it was finally capped.

An estimated 4.9 million barrels of oil escaped, making it the largest marine spill on record, and it fouled beaches and marshland from Texas to Florida. BP eventually agreed to pay over 20 billion dollars in fines and settlements, the largest corporate settlement in United States history.

A rock roughly ten kilometres across struck what is now the Yucatan Peninsula 66 million years ago, at Chicxulub, leaving a crater over 150 kilometres wide. The impact released energy equivalent to billions of Hiroshima bombs, triggered tsunamis and wildfires, and threw enough dust and sulphur into the atmosphere to block sunlight for months.

Roughly three quarters of species then living, including every non avian dinosaur, did not survive the resulting collapse of photosynthesis and the food chains built on it. Small feathered dinosaurs already living alongside their larger relatives were among the survivors, and their descendants are the birds now found on every continent.

Failed monsoons across the Deccan, Hyderabad, Gujarat and Marwar left fields barren through 1791 and into 1792, part of a longer drought lasting from 1789 to 1795. Grain reserves that might have cushioned earlier famines had already been drawn down, and starvation spread faster than relief could be organised across the affected princely states.

The famine became known in local memory as Doji Bara, the skull famine, because unburied bones were said to whiten the roads and fields for years afterward. One study estimates that around 11 million people died across the wider 1789 to 1792 drought period, a figure that cannot be broken down precisely by year or region because no single authority recorded deaths across the affected territories.

The passenger ferry Dona Paz collided with the oil tanker MT Vector in the Tablas Strait on the night of 20 December 1987, and Vector's cargo ignited, engulfing both vessels in fire. The ferry sank within about two hours; sharks reportedly took some of the survivors adrift in the water afterward.

Dona Paz was licensed to carry 1,518 passengers, but off-the-books ticket sales for the Christmas travel season meant close to 4,400 people are thought to have actually been aboard. A 1999 government report put the death toll at 4,385, with only 26 survivors, making it the deadliest peacetime maritime disaster on record.

Decades of ploughing had stripped the native grasses that once held the southern Plains soil in place, and when drought settled over Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas and neighbouring states in 1934, there was nothing left to stop the wind. Black Sunday, on 14 April 1935, brought a single storm that carried an estimated 300 million tons of topsoil as far as Chicago and New York.

Roughly 2.5 million people left the Plains during the decade, many for California, where they were derided as Okies regardless of which state they had actually come from. The disaster pushed Washington to fund large-scale soil conservation programmes, and the Soil Conservation Service, created in 1935, still shapes how American farmland is managed.

After Dutch railway workers struck in September 1944 to support the Allied advance, German occupation forces blocked food shipments into the still-occupied western Netherlands as punishment. An unusually early, hard winter froze the canals that many towns relied on for barge transport, cutting off what supplies remained.

Adult rations in cities such as Amsterdam and Rotterdam fell below 600 calories a day by early 1945, and roughly 20,000 people died before liberation in May. The famine later gave researchers a rare, closely dated natural experiment, and children conceived during those months showed measurably higher rates of heart disease and diabetes decades on.

The excursion steamer Eastland, chartered to carry Western Electric employees to a company picnic, rolled onto its side in the Chicago River on 24 July 1915 while still tied to the dock. The ship had a history of listing badly, and extra lifeboats added after new safety rules only made its top-heavy instability worse.

Many of the 844 dead drowned in the river's shallow water, trapped inside the hull or crushed under furniture as the ship rolled. It remains the deadliest single accident, by passengers lost, in Great Lakes shipping history.

Investigators later traced the outbreak to a single case in December 2013, a toddler in the Guinean village of Meliandou who is thought to have been infected by a bat. The virus spread into Conakry and across borders into Liberia and Sierra Leone before health authorities recognised it as Ebola the following March.

Over 11,000 people died out of more than 28,000 confirmed, probable and suspected cases, by far the largest Ebola outbreak recorded, and it overwhelmed health systems that had almost no isolation wards or trained staff to spare. A WHO-commissioned panel later concluded the agency itself had responded too slowly to declare an emergency.

The 1997 to 1998 El Nino formed as Pacific trade winds weakened and warm surface water piled up off South America, one of the two strongest such events on record alongside 1982 to 1983. Sea surface temperatures off Peru rose several degrees above normal, shifting rainfall patterns across the globe for the better part of a year.

It brought torrential flooding to Peru and East Africa, drought and wildfire haze across Indonesia, and an unusually mild, wet winter to the southern United States. Estimated global damage reached roughly 35 to 45 billion dollars, and the event sharpened forecasters' interest in El Nino as a driver of weather disasters worldwide, not a regional curiosity.

The Canadian Pacific liner Empress of Ireland collided with the Norwegian coal freighter Storstad in dense fog on the Saint Lawrence River on 29 May 1914. The Storstad's bow tore a hole below the Empress's waterline, and the ship rolled onto its side and sank in about 14 minutes.

Most passengers had no time to reach the boat deck; many drowned still asleep in their cabins below. The confirmed toll was 1,012, more than died on the Titanic two years earlier, though the disaster drew far less lasting attention because it broke two months before the First World War began.

The MS Estonia was sailing overnight from Tallinn to Stockholm on 28 September 1994 when its bow visor, the hinged door sealing the car deck, tore off in rough seas. Water flooded the deck within minutes, and the ship listed too far for most lifeboats to launch before it sank in the Baltic before dawn.

Of an estimated 989 people on board, 852 died, making it the deadliest peacetime shipping disaster in European waters since the Second World War. Investigators traced the failure to weak visor locks that had already been flagged as a design weakness on similar ferries. Sweden, Finland and Estonia later encased the wreck in concrete rather than raise it, treating the site as a grave.

Drought failed successive harvests across northern Ethiopia from 1983, and the ruling Derg government, fighting insurgencies in Tigray and Eritrea, restricted food movement into rebel-held areas and diverted resources to its military. Estimates of the dead range from 400,000 to over a million, a spread that reflects how little the government let outside observers count.

A BBC report by Michael Buerk in October 1984, describing Korem's camps as a biblical famine, reached global television audiences and prompted the Band Aid single and the Live Aid concerts of 1985. Relief aid reached millions, but much of it was also taxed and redirected by the government running the resettlement programmes that followed.

Temperatures across Western Europe climbed past 40 degrees Celsius in August 2003, the hottest summer the continent had recorded in centuries, and the heat lingered for weeks over cities with no tradition of air conditioning. Hospitals and morgues in France filled faster than staff could process the arrivals, many of them elderly people living alone.

A study covering 16 countries, published in the journal Comptes Rendus Biologies, counted over 70,000 excess deaths for the summer, with France and Italy each recording around 20,000. France's toll exposed gaps in checking on isolated elderly residents, and the government later created a national heat-warning system in response.

Extinction Rebellion, founded in the UK the previous year, staged its first major International Rebellion in April 2019, occupying five sites across central London, including Waterloo Bridge and Oxford Circus, for eleven days. Activists deliberately courted arrest, and London's Metropolitan Police made over 1,000 during the action, one of the largest mass-arrest operations the city had seen.

The group's three demands, that governments tell the truth about the climate emergency, cut emissions to net zero by 2025, and hand decisions to citizens' assemblies, spread to sister protests in cities including New York, Berlin and Sydney that same month. Parliament in Westminster declared a symbolic climate emergency days later, though the group's own 2025 target was not adopted by any national government.

The tanker Exxon Valdez ran aground on Bligh Reef in Alaska's Prince William Sound just after midnight on 24 March 1989, after the third mate, left in charge of the bridge, failed to turn the ship back into the shipping lane in time. It spilled roughly 11 million gallons of crude oil into waters that had until then been largely untouched by industry.

The oil eventually coated over 1,300 miles of coastline and killed hundreds of thousands of seabirds along with otters, seals and orcas. Exxon's cleanup and legal costs ran into billions of dollars, and a punitive damages case over the spill reached the United States Supreme Court in 2008, which cut the original jury award substantially.

An unusually cold, wet summer in 1866 rotted potatoes in the ground and left grain unable to ripen before autumn frosts across Finland, then part of the Russian Empire. Harvests failed again the following two years, and roads in the hardest-hit provinces of Ostrobothnia, Tavastia and North Karelia filled with people walking in search of food or work.

About 270,000 people died across the three famine years, roughly 150,000 more than normal mortality would predict, and around 8.5 percent of the entire population, rising to about 20 percent in the worst-hit districts. It is generally regarded as the last famine in Europe caused primarily by weather rather than war or blockade, and it pushed Finland's government toward building railways and grain reserves to prevent a recurrence.

The Fukushima Daiichi plant survived the magnitude 9.0 Tōhoku earthquake of 11 March 2011, but the tsunami that followed overtopped its seawall and flooded the diesel generators that cooled the reactors. Without power, three of the six reactors overheated and their fuel partially melted within days, and hydrogen explosions tore open two reactor buildings.

Roughly 150,000 people were evacuated from the surrounding area, some for years. The International Atomic Energy Agency ranked it a level 7 event, the same top rating given to Chernobyl, though Fukushima released far less radioactive material and no deaths were directly attributed to radiation exposure.

A hurricane struck Galveston, Texas, on 8 September 1900 with a storm surge that put most of the low, unwalled island underwater. The Weather Bureau had downplayed warnings from Cuban forecasters who had tracked the storm more accurately, and the city had no seawall to slow the surge.

Estimates of the dead range from about 6,000 to 12,000, a spread that reflects how many bodies were never recovered from the Gulf; contemporary tallies by the Galveston Relief Committee settled near 8,000. The disaster prompted construction of a 17-foot seawall and a citywide grade-raising project completed over the following decade.

The paddle steamer General Slocum caught fire on 15 June 1904 while carrying members of a German Lutheran congregation, mostly women and children, to a church picnic on Long Island. Crew failed a fire drill that had never actually been held, and the lifebelts crumbled when tested, having rotted for years.

The captain steered toward North Brother Island rather than the nearer shore, fanning the flames, and many passengers drowned in the East River wearing lifebelts that had disintegrated. The death toll, tallied by the coroner's office, was 1,021, making it New York's deadliest disaster before the September 11 attacks.

Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy on 15 September 2008, the largest corporate collapse in American history, after years of subprime mortgage lending had built a bond market nobody could accurately price. Credit markets froze within days, and banks stopped lending even to each other because none could tell which of them was insolvent.

Governments that had just watched Lehman fail spent the following weeks bailing out banks they judged too large to lose, including AIG and much of Britain's high street lending. Unemployment in the United States rose past ten percent by 2009, and the recovery in household wealth took most of the following decade.

A fire broke out in Boston on 20 March 1760, starting in a dockside tavern and spreading through the tightly packed wooden buildings of the town's commercial waterfront. It burned through the night and destroyed roughly 349 buildings, one of the largest urban fires in colonial North America before the Revolution, leaving an estimated one in ten Bostonians homeless.

Benjamin Franklin, then in London, helped raise relief funds from English donors for the rebuilding, an early instance of transatlantic disaster relief. The fire pushed Boston toward stricter building codes favouring brick over wood, though it took further large fires in the following century to make brick construction the rule rather than the exception.

The fire broke out on the evening of 8 October 1871, reportedly near a barn on De Koven Street, and spread rapidly through a city built largely of wood, including wooden sidewalks and shingle roofs, during a hot, dry autumn with strong southwesterly winds. It burned for about two days before rain helped bring it under control on 10 October.

The blaze destroyed roughly three and a half square miles of the city, including most of its central business district, and left about 100,000 people, a third of Chicago's population, without homes. Around 300 people are estimated to have died, a comparatively low figure given the destruction, and the rebuilding that followed made Chicago a testing ground for early steel-frame skyscraper construction.

Rain fell across northern Europe through the spring and summer of 1315 and did not let up, drowning fields from Ireland to Poland for three consecutive growing seasons. Grain prices tripled and quadrupled in places, seed corn was eaten rather than sown, and reports from English and French chronicles describe people eating cats, dogs and, in a few desperate accounts, each other.

Historians estimate that roughly ten to fifteen percent of the population of northern Europe died between 1315 and 1317, concentrated among the peasantry who had no reserves to draw on. It weakened the same population that the Black Death would strike a generation later, and some historians treat the famine as the point at which medieval Europe's long agricultural expansion ran out.

The fire began in a baker's shop on Pudding Lane in the early hours of 2 September 1666 and, driven by a strong east wind through streets of timber-framed, pitch-caulked houses packed tightly along the Thames, burned for four days. It destroyed most of the walled City of London, including old St Paul's Cathedral and roughly 13,000 houses, and left an estimated 70,000 to 100,000 people homeless.

Only a handful of deaths were officially recorded, though historians think the real toll was higher and simply went uncounted among London's poor. The rebuilding that followed, overseen in part by Christopher Wren, replaced the old wooden city with brick and stone and gave London the network of churches, including a new St Paul's, that still shapes its skyline.

A fire broke out on the night of 16 December 1835 in a warehouse on Merchant Street in lower Manhattan, and bitter cold that had frozen the East River hampered firefighters trying to draw water through iced-over hydrants and cisterns. Winds spread the flames through the financial district's densely packed stores and offices before crews finally stopped it by dynamiting buildings to create a firebreak.

Around 700 buildings burned, wiping out most of the commercial district south of Wall Street, and losses were estimated at roughly 20 million dollars in 1835 money. The fire bankrupted most of the city's fire insurance companies, since nearly all of them held policies concentrated in the same few burned blocks, New York rebuilt the district with wider streets and less flammable construction.

Fire broke out among the shops near Rome's Circus Maximus in July of the year 64 and burned for about six days, gutting narrow, densely built neighbourhoods before it was brought under control. Ten of the city's fourteen districts were damaged, and the historian Tacitus, writing decades later, is the main surviving source for how it spread.

The rumour that the emperor Nero started the fire to clear land for a new palace, or fiddled while it burned, has no reliable contemporary support. Tacitus records that Nero blamed the city's Christians instead, and had some tortured and executed for it, an episode later writers treated as the start of Roman persecution of the faith.

The Great Hurricane of 1780 crossed the eastern Caribbean between 9 and 15 October, striking Barbados, Martinique, Saint Lucia and Sint Eustatius while British and French fleets were fighting nearby during the American Revolutionary War. Barbados lost most of its buildings, and warships on both sides were wrecked or driven ashore, thinning the naval forces each side had committed to the region.

Estimates of the dead run from around 20,000 to over 25,000, the highest toll of any Atlantic hurricane on record, with roughly 9,000 deaths on Martinique and 6,000 on Saint Lucia among the worst-hit islands. A large share of the deaths came afterwards, from the starvation that followed when the storm destroyed the season's food crops across the islands.

The earthquake struck at 11:58 am on 1 September 1923, near lunchtime, when many households had open cooking fires burning. Those fires spread through Tokyo and Yokohama's wooden buildings faster than the quake damage itself, and a firestorm at one Tokyo clothing depot killed roughly 38,000 people sheltering there in a single afternoon.

Estimates of the total dead range from about 105,000 to 140,000, figures compiled from municipal and police records that never fully accounted for the missing. In the panic afterward, rumours blaming Koreans for arson and well poisoning spread through Tokyo, and vigilante groups and police killed an estimated several thousand ethnic Koreans in the following days.

The famine followed the Great Leap Forward, Mao Zedong's 1958 push to collectivise farms and shift labour into backyard steel furnaces, which drew workers away from harvests just as local officials inflated grain output figures to please Beijing. Those inflated reports set procurement quotas too high, so villages that had already fallen short still had grain requisitioned out from under them.

Historians' estimates of the dead range from about 15 million to 45 million, the wide spread reflecting how long China's own archives stayed closed and how deaths were classified between starvation, disease and violence. The demographer Judith Banister and later the historian Frank Dikotter, working from provincial records opened after 1980, produced the higher figures now most widely cited.

Bubonic plague had never fully left London after the Black Death, breaking out in smaller waves roughly every generation, but the outbreak that began in the parish of St Giles-in-the-Fields in early 1665 grew into the city's worst in decades. Parish clerks recorded weekly burials in printed Bills of Mortality, which let Londoners watch the death count climb in something close to real time, a practice unusual for its era.

The official toll was near 68,000, though the true figure is generally put closer to 100,000 given how many deaths went unrecorded, particularly among the poor who fled or died unnoticed. The wealthy who could leave London did so, King Charles II's court relocated to Oxford, and the outbreak eased over the winter of 1665 to 1666, only weeks before the Great Fire swept through the city.

A cold spell in early December 1952 led Londoners to burn more coal than usual, and a temperature inversion trapped the resulting smoke and sulphur dioxide low over the city for five days. Visibility fell so far that buses ran with a conductor walking ahead carrying a light, and some indoor cinema and theatre performances were cancelled because smog seeped inside the buildings.

Contemporary reports counted around 4,000 excess deaths, mostly from respiratory failure among infants, the elderly and those with existing chest conditions. Later statistical reanalysis, comparing the weeks after the smog rather than just during it, put the toll closer to 12,000. The event led directly to Britain's Clean Air Act of 1956.

The fire that broke out in a fourth-floor flat at Grenfell Tower in North Kensington, London, in the early hours of 14 June 2017 started in a faulty fridge freezer, an ordinary domestic fault. It spread up the outside of the 24-storey block within minutes because a recent refurbishment had clad the building in combustible panels.

72 residents died, many of them following official advice to stay in their flats rather than evacuate, a policy designed for buildings that do not burn like Grenfell did. A public inquiry later found the cladding had been chosen partly on cost and that safety warnings from residents had gone unheeded for years.

The magnitude 7.5 earthquake struck early on 4 February 1976 along the Motagua fault, which runs across Guatemala's highlands, at a time when most residents in rural towns lived in adobe brick houses with heavy tile roofs. Those buildings collapsed inward on sleeping occupants far more often than the reinforced structures common in the capital.

The quake killed an estimated 23,000 people and injured around 76,000, with damage concentrated in poorer rural departments outside Guatemala City rather than the capital itself. It prompted a rebuilding effort that promoted lighter roofing and reinforced construction, aimed specifically at the adobe housing that had caused most of the deaths.

A magnitude 7.0 earthquake struck near Port-au-Prince on 12 January 2010, its epicentre only about 25 kilometres from the capital, and toppled the presidential palace, the cathedral and much of the city's poorly reinforced concrete housing within seconds. The government initially reported around 230,000 dead, then revised the figure upward to 316,000.

That later number is disputed. Independent researchers and a 2010 study in Medicine, Conflict and Survival put the likely toll closer to 158,000, and no full count was ever possible because bodies were cleared from the streets in a rushed, chaotic operation. Well over a million survivors were left homeless in tent camps for years afterward.

An earthquake estimated at magnitude 8.3 struck Haiyuan county in Ningxia, northwestern China, on 16 December 1920, triggering landslides in the region's thick loess soil that buried entire villages. Some settlements were simply gone beneath collapsed hillsides by morning.

Chinese studies published since 2010 put the toll between roughly 259,000 and 273,000; the US Geological Survey has used a more conservative figure of 200,000. News of the disaster reached the outside world only slowly, over weeks, because the region had almost no telegraph lines.

The French cargo ship Mont-Blanc, loaded with wartime high explosives, collided with the Norwegian vessel Imo in Halifax Harbour on the morning of 6 December 1917. Its crew abandoned ship and rowed for shore as the burning Mont-Blanc drifted toward the docks, drawing crowds of onlookers to their windows.

The ship detonated roughly twenty minutes later in the largest human-made explosion before the nuclear age, flattening the Richmond district and shattering windows for kilometres, blinding many who had been watching from indoors. Estimates of the dead range from about 1,800 to 2,000, drawn from relief commission burial records.

Lake Taupo in New Zealand's North Island sits over the vent of an eruption around 180 CE that geologists rank among the most violent anywhere in the past 5,000 years. It ejected roughly 100 cubic kilometres of material and produced a pyroclastic flow that reportedly reddened skies as far away as Rome and China, according to later chronicled accounts of unusual sunsets.

New Zealand was uninhabited by people at the time, since Polynesian settlement did not begin for another thousand years, so the eruption left no human death toll to record. What survives instead is a landscape: the present lake fills the caldera left behind, and layers of ignimbrite from the event are still used to date archaeological sites across the island.

Before an FA Cup semi-final at Sheffield's Hillsborough stadium on 15 April 1989, police opened an exit gate to relieve crowding outside, and the surge of arriving Liverpool supporters funnelled into an already packed standing terrace with no way out through its perimeter fencing. Ninety-seven people died from crush injuries, most within minutes.

Police initially blamed drunk and violent fans, a version repeated in press coverage at the time, and an inquest jury was directed to disregard events after 3:15pm, when most victims were already fatally injured. A 2016 inquest finally ruled the deaths unlawful killing, finding failures by South Yorkshire Police were the main cause.

The Hindenburg had already made ten round trips across the Atlantic without incident when it caught fire while mooring at Naval Air Station Lakehurst, New Jersey, on 6 May 1937. The airship burned and fell to the ground in under a minute, and radio announcer Herbert Morrison's recorded, unscripted commentary, describing the flames live, became the disaster's defining record.

Thirty five of the 97 people aboard died, along with one member of the ground crew. The cause was never settled with certainty, though a static spark igniting leaking hydrogen is the leading explanation. Public confidence in hydrogen airships collapsed with the wreck, and no passenger airship of that scale flew again.

In 1932 and 1933, Soviet authorities set grain quotas for Ukraine far above what its farms could produce after forced collectivisation, then enforced those quotas with searches, blacklists on villages that fell short, and a ban on peasants leaving to seek food elsewhere. Grain that could have fed the region was exported or stockpiled while famine spread through the countryside.

Demographers' estimates of the dead range from about 3.5 million to five million, drawn from Soviet census gaps rather than any contemporary count, since the state denied a famine was occurring at all. Ukraine and more than twenty other countries now formally recognise the famine as a genocide, a term first argued for by the lawyer Raphael Lemkin, who coined the word itself partly with this famine in mind.

The pandemic strain, H3N2, was first detected in Hong Kong in July 1968 and had reached the United States by September, spread largely by returning Vietnam War troops and by international air travel that was faster and busier than during the 1957 pandemic. It replaced the earlier H2N2 strain as the dominant circulating flu and its descendants still circulate seasonally.

Global deaths are estimated at roughly one to four million, a wide range reflecting inconsistent national reporting rather than any single revised count. Mortality fell most heavily on the elderly, and because H3N2 shared some features with the 1957 strain, prior exposure to Asian flu appears to have given some older adults partial protection.

Huaynaputina, a volcano in southern Peru with no recorded history of eruption, exploded on 19 February 1600 and buried nearby towns under metres of ash and pyroclastic debris. It remains the largest volcanic eruption known to have occurred in South America, and it killed at least 1,500 people in the immediate region, mostly from ash falls and the pyroclastic flows that reached the Pacific coast.

Tree rings and ice cores show the eruption's sulphate cloud spreading around the globe, and 1601 was later identified as one of the coldest years of the last six centuries in the northern hemisphere. Contemporary Spanish colonial accounts from Arequipa, buried under ash for days, gave later researchers a firm date to match against the climate record.

Andrew crossed the Bahamas and struck south of Miami on 24 August 1992 as a Category 5 storm, with sustained winds estimated near 165 mph. It flattened whole subdivisions in Homestead and Florida City in under four hours, and its landfall pressure was one of the lowest ever recorded for an Atlantic hurricane at the time.

It killed 65 people and left roughly 250,000 temporarily homeless, damage that state and federal officials estimated near 25 billion dollars. The building failures it exposed, roofs and walls stripped from houses built to code, forced Florida to rewrite its statewide building code in 2001 with stricter wind and impact standards.

Katrina made landfall near New Orleans on 29 August 2005, but the storm surge itself was not what flooded the city; the levees and floodwalls protecting it failed in more than fifty places, and water kept rising for hours after the winds had passed. Roughly 80 percent of New Orleans ended up underwater, some neighbourhoods under ten feet or more.

The disaster killed over 1,800 people across the Gulf Coast and displaced more than a million, and the slow federal response, especially in the majority-Black Lower Ninth Ward, became a lasting point of criticism of FEMA and the Bush administration. The Army Corps of Engineers, which had built the levees, later acknowledged design flaws in the system that failed.

Mitch peaked as a Category 5 hurricane in the western Caribbean in late October 1998, then stalled over Honduras for days, dumping rainfall measured in feet rather than inches. Its slow crawl, rather than its peak winds, did most of the damage: mountainsides gave way and rivers buried whole villages under mud.

Estimates put the dead at over 11,000 across Honduras and Nicaragua, with thousands more never found. No Atlantic storm had killed on that scale since the Great Hurricane of 1780. It set back Honduras's economy by years, destroying roughly 70 percent of its crops and much of its road network, and prompted a wave of migration north that outlasted the storm by decades.

Hurricane Sandy formed in the Caribbean in October 2012 and grew unusually wide as it curved north, merging with a separate winter storm system before striking the New Jersey coast on 29 October. Its storm surge flooded the New York City subway system and lower Manhattan, and left large parts of the region without power for days.

Sandy caused more than 230 deaths across eight countries, including at least 71 in the northeastern United States, and roughly 70 billion dollars in damage, making it one of the costliest storms in American history at the time. Its size, over 1,600 kilometres across at landfall, was as unusual as its intensity, and it prompted New York and New Jersey to invest heavily in coastal flood defences afterwards.

Eyjafjallajokull, a modest ice-capped volcano in southern Iceland, began erupting explosively on 14 April 2010 after meltwater from its overlying glacier met the rising magma. The resulting steam shattered the lava into an unusually fine ash that was carried high into the jet stream by prevailing winds.

European aviation authorities, wary of ash damaging jet engines after past close calls, closed most of the continent's airspace for about a week, grounding over 100,000 flights and stranding an estimated eight to ten million travellers. It was the largest disruption to European air travel since the Second World War, and it prompted airlines to press for less cautious ash-density thresholds afterwards.

A magnitude 9.1 earthquake ruptured off the coast of Sumatra on 26 December 2004, one of the largest ever recorded, displacing the seafloor enough to send waves racing across the entire Indian Ocean. Coastal communities in Indonesia's Aceh province had almost no warning; the waves arrived within twenty minutes of the quake.

The tsunami killed over 230,000 people across fourteen countries, with Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India and Thailand hit hardest, and it displaced well over a million more. No basin-wide tsunami warning system existed for the Indian Ocean at the time; the disaster led directly to one being built, with sensor buoys and coastal alert networks installed across the region in the years that followed.

Drought struck the coastal Odisha region in 1865, and by the time colonial officials recognised the scale of the crop failure and moved to import rice, the monsoon of 1866 had arrived and closed the port of Cuttack to grain shipments for months. Relief that could have reached the region earlier was delayed by administrators who doubted the severity of reports coming from local officers.

Estimates for the dead in Odisha alone range from about 800,000 to a million people out of a population of roughly three million, close to a third of the region, with millions more affected across the wider famine zone. The disaster prompted the colonial government's first Famine Commission, which set out early principles for famine relief that were only inconsistently applied in later famines.

A magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck the Alborz mountains of northern Iran on 21 June 1990, centred near the towns of Rudbar and Manjil, and was followed within minutes by a second strong shock that brought down buildings already weakened by the first. Landslides in the steep terrain buried entire villages.

Estimates of the dead range from around 35,000 to 50,000, a spread reflecting the difficulty of counting victims in remote, mountainous communities where whole settlements were destroyed at once. Hundreds of thousands more were left homeless, and the disaster prompted a rare period of Iranian acceptance of Western humanitarian aid.

The winter of 1740 to 1741 brought extreme cold across Ireland, part of a wider European cold spell, freezing rivers and destroying the potato and grain crops that much of the country depended on. Unlike the famine of the following century, this one left no widespread visual record and little literary memory, which is part of why historians now call it forgotten.

Estimates of the dead range from roughly 13 to 40 percent of Ireland's population, a proportional toll that some historians argue was worse than the better-known famine of the 1840s, though the smaller total population of the 1740s means the absolute number of dead was lower. Cold, not blight, was the direct cause, killing livestock and crops alike before famine and disease finished the work.

A fungus called Phytophthora infestans reached Ireland in the autumn of 1845, rotting potato plants in the field within days and destroying much of that year's crop; the disease returned even more severely in 1846 and periodically through 1852. Potatoes were the primary food of roughly a third of Ireland's population, tenant farmers who had little land to grow anything else on.

Ireland's population fell by an estimated one to one and a half million deaths from starvation and disease, and by a further million or more through emigration, chiefly to Britain and North America. Ireland continued exporting grain and livestock through the worst famine years under its tenancy and trade arrangements with Britain, a fact that shaped Irish nationalist politics for generations afterward.

Plague reached Lombardy in 1629 carried by troops moving through northern Italy during the Thirty Years War, and from Milan it spread south through Venice, Verona and much of the peninsula over the following two years. Alessandro Manzoni later drew on Milanese archives of the outbreak for his novel The Betrothed, giving the epidemic a wider afterlife than most plague years of the period.

Estimates of the dead across northern and central Italy run above a million people, with Milan and Venice among the hardest hit cities, each losing a large share of their population within months. Civic authorities imposed quarantines and burned the belongings of the dead, measures that slowed but did not stop a disease whose cause, the bacterium carried by fleas on rats, would not be identified for another two and a half centuries.

Japan Airlines Flight 123 suffered a sudden decompression twelve minutes after leaving Tokyo's Haneda Airport on 12 August 1985, when its rear pressure bulkhead failed and tore away most of the vertical tail fin, severing all four hydraulic lines. The crew fought the crippled 747 for 32 minutes using only engine thrust before it crashed into a mountainside near Mount Takamagahara.

Of 524 people on board, 520 died, making it the deadliest single-aircraft accident in aviation history. Investigators traced the failure to a faulty repair Boeing had made to the same aircraft seven years earlier after a tailstrike, where a doubler plate had been riveted rather than fitted to specification, allowing metal fatigue to spread undetected.

The Joelma building, a 25-storey office tower in downtown Sao Paulo, caught fire on 1 February 1974 when an overloaded air conditioning unit on the twelfth floor overheated. Brazilian building codes at the time did not require fire escapes, sprinklers or fireproof stairwells in towers of that size, and the building had none.

Smoke filled the stairwells within minutes, trapping office workers on upper floors with no way down; some jumped or were killed by falling debris, others died of smoke inhalation. The fire killed 189 people and injured close to 300, and it led directly to Sao Paulo's first modern fire safety codes for high-rise construction.

The South Fork Dam, holding back Lake Conemaugh 14 miles above Johnstown, had been patched with materials that reduced its spillway capacity. Heavy rain on 31 May 1889 sent the dam over the top, and it collapsed that afternoon, releasing about twenty million tons of water down the valley.

The wave reached Johnstown within an hour, carrying houses, rail cars and barbed wire from a wire works into a stone bridge, where debris caught fire. The Pennsylvania Railroad's owners, the same wealthy sportsmen who had bought the dam and neglected its repair, faced lawsuits but no successful judgment. The death toll, compiled from burial and coroner records, stands at 2,209.

On 18 November 1978, more than 900 members of the Peoples Temple died at Jim Jones's jungle settlement in Guyana, most from a drink laced with cyanide, sedatives and powdered fruit juice. Nurses and parents dosed infants and children first with syringes. Armed guards stood at the pavilion's edges as adults were told to follow.

The killing came hours after Jones's followers had ambushed and shot Congressman Leo Ryan, who had flown in to investigate, at a nearby airstrip, killing him and four others. Jones was found dead in his chair from a gunshot wound, most likely self-inflicted. Over 200 of the dead were children, and the toll remains the largest single loss of American civilian life from a deliberate act before 2001.

The plague that first struck Constantinople in 541 CE returned in repeated waves for the next two centuries, and one severe recurrence hit the Sasanian Persian Empire around 627 CE, during the final Byzantine Sasanian war. The outbreak is named for Kavad II, known as Sheroe, the Sasanian king who took the throne that year after murdering his father, Khosrow II.

Kavad II himself is generally reported to have died of the plague within months of seizing power, after a reign of only weeks, leaving the empire in a succession crisis it never fully recovered from. Persian sources describe the disease reaching the capital, Ctesiphon, though no reliable death toll survives from the period.

The earthquake struck on 8 October 2005, its magnitude 7.6 rupture centred near Muzaffarabad in Pakistan-administered Kashmir. It hit mid-morning, when schools were in session, and poorly reinforced concrete school buildings collapsed on students by the thousands across the region's mountainous districts.

Pakistani officials counted more than 73,000 dead, while later estimates ran as high as 87,000 once deaths in Indian-administered Kashmir were included, and over 3 million people were left homeless as winter approached in the Himalayan foothills. The remoteness of the terrain slowed relief for weeks, and the disaster prompted a brief, unusual period of cross-border cooperation between Pakistan and India.

A blizzard dropped 28 inches of snow on Washington D.C. between 27 and 29 January 1922, the heaviest snowfall the city had recorded. On the evening of the 28th, about 500 people were inside the Knickerbocker Theatre in Adams Morgan watching the silent comedy Get-Rich-Quick Wallingford when the weight of accumulated snow brought the roof down.

Ninety-eight people died and 133 were injured, including several members of Congress and local officials. Investigators found the contractor had set the roof's steel support beams only two inches into the walls instead of the eight specified in the design. The collapse led directly to stricter building codes for flat roofs in the district.

The earthquake struck before dawn on 17 January 1995, its magnitude 6.9 rupture running beneath the port city of Kobe. Older wooden houses with heavy tile roofs collapsed onto their occupants by the thousands, and elevated highways and rail lines built before modern seismic codes buckled or fell.

More than 6,400 people died and over 100,000 buildings were destroyed, in Japan's deadliest earthquake since 1923. The slow initial response, hampered by blocked roads and a government criticised for delaying help, pushed Japan to overhaul disaster response and building codes, and the rebuilt port reopened within two years.

Four explosions tore through Krakatoa on the morning of 27 August 1883, the loudest at 10:02 a.m. registering as the loudest sound ever recorded by human ears, heard in Perth, nearly 2,000 miles away, and on Rodrigues Island, 3,000 miles out in the Indian Ocean. More than two thirds of the island collapsed into the caldera the blast tore open beneath it.

Most of the roughly 36,000 dead drowned, pushed under by waves the collapse threw up, some reaching 41 metres, that swept the coasts of Java and Sumatra. A smaller share, put at around a tenth, were killed onshore by pyroclastic flows that crossed open water and burned fishing villages. A new cone, Anak Krakatau, broke the surface of the same caldera in the late 1920s and still erupts.

On 8 August 2023, wildfires fanned by a passing hurricane's winds and a landscape of dry invasive grasses swept through Lahaina, the former capital of the Hawaiian kingdom, on the island of Maui. Downed power lines are thought to have sparked the blaze, which moved fast enough to trap people in cars and in the water offshore as they fled.

Maui County's confirmed death toll stood at 102 by mid-2024, revised down from an earlier estimate of up to 115 once DNA testing showed some remains had been counted twice. It was the deadliest wildfire in the United States in more than a century, and it destroyed nearly all of Lahaina's historic town centre.

Lake Nyos sits in the crater of an extinct volcano in Cameroon, and carbon dioxide had been seeping into its bottom waters from magma below for years, held there by pressure like an unopened bottle of soda. On the night of 21 August 1986, something, possibly a landslide, disturbed the lake enough to release the gas in a single overturning event.

A cloud of roughly 100,000 to 300,000 tonnes of CO2 rolled down two valleys at speeds up to 100 kilometres an hour, displacing breathable air and asphyxiating around 1,700 people and thousands of cattle in nearby villages, some as far as 25 kilometres away. Survivors described a smell like gunpowder and animals dropping before humans understood what was happening.

Laki, a volcanic fissure in southern Iceland, opened along a 27-kilometre crack in June 1783 and kept erupting for eight months, releasing enormous quantities of sulphur dioxide and fluorine along with its lava. The fluorine poisoned grazing land across Iceland, killing more than half the country's livestock within a year and bringing on a famine that, by 1785, had killed roughly a fifth of the Icelandic population.

The eruption's haze drifted over Europe that summer as a persistent dry fog, and parish burial records in England and France show a marked rise in deaths, likely from the sulphurous air itself rather than famine. Poor harvests in the following years, sometimes linked to the eruption, have been cited among the pressures building toward the French Revolution six years later.
