Pollen records, lake sediment cores and cave stalagmites from Cyprus, Syria and the Aegean show a marked dry period beginning around 1200 BCE and lasting a century or more, coinciding with the wider collapse of eastern Mediterranean states. Reduced rainfall would have cut grain yields sharply in a region that already depended on imported cereals.

Hittite letters from the period ask Egypt for emergency grain shipments, which fits the drought evidence, though it is one strand among several: warfare, migration and trade breakdown were happening at the same time. Climate scientists reconstruct the drought's severity from oxygen isotopes rather than any single written account.

An earthquake struck Lisbon on the morning of 1 November 1755, All Saints' Day, while much of the city's population was inside churches for mass. The shaking, estimated above magnitude 8.5, was followed within an hour by a tsunami up to several metres high that drowned survivors who had fled to the waterfront, and then by fires that burned through the ruins for days.

Estimates of the dead in Lisbon alone range from 12,000 to over 50,000, out of a city of around 200,000, with the wide range reflecting how much of the record itself was destroyed. The Portuguese chief minister, the Marquis of Pombal, organised relief and rebuilt the city on a new grid plan, and philosophers across Europe, including Voltaire, cited the disaster in arguments against the idea that the world was inherently well ordered.

A bomb hidden inside a radio-cassette player in checked luggage exploded aboard Pan Am Flight 103 on 21 December 1988, thirty-eight minutes after it left London Heathrow for New York. The Boeing 747 broke apart at 31,000 feet over the Scottish town of Lockerbie, scattering wreckage and bodies across the countryside and into houses on Sherwood Crescent.

All 259 people aboard died along with 11 residents on the ground, killed when a wing section landed on their homes and exploded, for a total of 270 victims. Libyan intelligence officer Abdelbaset al-Megrahi was convicted of the bombing in 2001 after an investigation that traced fragments of the bomb's timer to a circuit board sold to Libya.

On 17 October 1814, an iron hoop failed on a vat holding roughly 3,500 barrels of porter at the Horse Shoe Brewery on London's Tottenham Court Road. The vat's collapse ruptured neighbouring vats and casks, and more than 320,000 litres of beer burst through a brewery wall into the slum housing of St Giles.

The wave of beer flooded cellars where families lived below street level and collapsed at least two houses, killing eight people, mostly women and children, by drowning or injury. The brewery was taken to court but faced no penalty, since the flood was ruled an act of God, and it later reclaimed some losses through a rebate on beer duty already paid.

A new coronavirus was isolated from a patient in Saudi Arabia in September 2012, though later tracing found an earlier case in Jordan that April. The virus causes severe respiratory illness with a fatality rate far higher than seasonal flu, and most infections were eventually linked to contact with dromedary camels, which carry the virus without symptoms.

Later surveys found the virus in most of Saudi Arabia's camel herds, some going back decades, suggesting camels had carried MERS long before it was noticed in humans. A 2015 outbreak traced to a single traveller returning from the Middle East infected 186 people in South Korea, mostly inside crowded hospital wards.

An earthquake near magnitude 7.1 struck the Strait of Messina before dawn on 28 December 1908, followed within minutes by a tsunami up to 12 metres high that drowned survivors who had fled onto the shore. Messina and Reggio Calabria, on opposite sides of the strait, were both largely destroyed.

Estimates of the dead range from about 75,000 to over 100,000, figures compiled from Italian government surveys taken amid a collapsed local administration, with some later accounts citing numbers as high as 200,000. Russian and British naval crews docked nearby provided some of the earliest organised rescue efforts.

A magnitude 8.0 earthquake struck off Mexico's Pacific coast on 19 September 1985, and the shaking arrived in the capital, 350 kilometres away, amplified by the soft lakebed sediment the city is built on. Whole blocks of mid-rise buildings pancaked in the historic centre while structures on firmer ground nearby stood largely untouched.

Official counts put the dead at around 10,000, though some estimates run higher, and the government's slow, understaffed response pushed ordinary residents into forming their own rescue brigades, some digging survivors from the rubble of the General Hospital with hand tools. The quake's date is now marked annually with a national earthquake drill.

Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 lost contact with air traffic control less than an hour after leaving Kuala Lumpur for Beijing on 8 March 2014, and its transponder went dark soon after. Satellite handshake data later showed the Boeing 777 had turned sharply off course and flown south for hours into the Indian Ocean.

None of the 239 people aboard were found, and only a few dozen pieces of debris, some confirmed as belonging to the plane, ever washed ashore, the first on Réunion Island in 2015. A search of the ocean floor covering over 120,000 square kilometres failed to locate the wreck, and the case remains unresolved.

Doctors in the fishing town of Minamata, Japan, began reporting patients with slurred speech, tremors and loss of coordination in 1956, and some children were born with severe developmental disabilities. Cats in the area had been dying in convulsions for years before the human cases were formally recognised, a warning sign locals had noticed but doctors had not yet connected.

The cause was traced to methylmercury discharged into Minamata Bay by the Chisso chemical company, which had been dumping industrial wastewater into the bay since the 1930s. Mercury accumulated in fish that formed the local diet, and Chisso continued discharging the waste for years after the link was suspected, denying responsibility until a 1973 court ruling forced compensation.

The only account comes from Gabriele de Mussis, a notary in Piacenza who never set foot in Caffa himself. Writing around 1348 from stories told by returning merchants, he says the Mongols flung their own plague dead over the walls in early 1346, hoping panic and the stench would break the siege.

Most historians now doubt the corpses did much of the work. Plague travels in fleas riding on rats, not in flung bodies, and Genoese ships kept crossing the Black Sea regardless of the fighting. That traffic carried the disease to Constantinople by 1347 and to Messina, Sicily, that October, aboard twelve galleys already crewed by the dying.

On 18 May 1980, a magnitude 5.1 earthquake triggered the largest landslide in recorded history off the north face of Mount St. Helens in Washington State, uncorking a lateral blast that flattened forest across roughly 600 square kilometres in minutes. The volcano's summit dropped by around 400 metres.

Fifty-seven people died, among them volcanologist David Johnston, who radioed a final warning from his observation post eight kilometres away, and Harry Truman, an 83-year-old lodge owner who had refused for weeks to leave his home on Spirit Lake. Ash fell across eleven states, and the eruption became the costliest and deadliest in United States history.

Mount Tarawera, on New Zealand's North Island, erupted just after midnight on 10 June 1886, splitting open along a line more than 17 kilometres long and throwing ash, rock and mud over the surrounding countryside. The eruption obliterated several Maori villages, including Te Wairoa, and buried the Pink and White Terraces, silica rock formations on the shore of nearby Lake Rotomahana that had drawn tourists from around the world.

At least 120 people died, most of them Maori residents of the villages nearest the mountain, making it New Zealand's deadliest eruption on record. The Terraces themselves were long assumed destroyed outright, though geologists in the twenty-first century have argued that submerged remnants of them may still survive beneath the enlarged lake.

Before dawn on 5 September 1972, eight members of the Palestinian group Black September climbed a fence into the Olympic Village in Munich and took nine Israeli athletes and coaches hostage after killing two others in the initial struggle. West German police, with no trained hostage negotiators or tactical unit for such a siege, tried to talk terms through the day.

That night, during a botched rescue attempt at Furstenfeldbruck airfield where the hostage takers had been offered a flight out, all nine remaining hostages were killed, along with five of the eight hostage takers and one police officer. West Germany later formed its GSG 9 counter-terrorism unit directly in response to the failure, and Israel launched a long covert campaign against those it held responsible for planning the attack.

Neanderthals had lived across Europe and western Asia for over 300,000 years before their population fell to undetectable levels around 40,000 years ago, not long after modern humans expanded into the same territory. The last confirmed sites, including caves in Gibraltar and Croatia, show no single catastrophe, just a slow retreat.

Genetic studies show the two groups interbred, and most living humans outside Africa carry a small percentage of Neanderthal DNA, so the species did not vanish without trace. Proposed causes, competition for resources, a smaller population's vulnerability to disease, and a cooling climate, are not mutually exclusive, and researchers now generally treat extinction as the result of several pressures acting together.

The earthquake struck on 15 January 1934 with a magnitude near 8.0, its epicentre in eastern Nepal close to the Bihar border. Large parts of Kathmandu and the Bihar city of Munger were destroyed, and sections of the Ganges plain around Bihar sank or liquefied, swallowing whole buildings into suddenly soft ground.

Estimates place the dead between 6,000 and 10,700, figures assembled separately by Nepalese and British Indian authorities, since Nepal was then an isolated kingdom that limited outside access. A young Mahatma Gandhi visited the Bihar disaster zone afterward and controversially described the quake as divine punishment for the practice of untouchability, a claim Rabindranath Tagore publicly rejected.

A magnitude 7.8 earthquake centred near the town of Gorkha struck Nepal on 25 April 2015, the country's worst in over eighty years, and triggered avalanches on Everest that killed climbers at base camp. Kathmandu's Dharahara tower, a nineteenth-century landmark, collapsed with tourists still inside it.

Nearly 9,000 people died and hundreds of thousands of homes were destroyed, many of them stone and mud houses in remote mountain districts that took months to reach with aid. Temples and palaces across the Kathmandu Valley, several dating back centuries, were reduced to rubble alongside the modern housing around them.

Nevado del Ruiz erupted on the evening of 13 November 1985, and its pyroclastic flows melted part of the ice cap high above the Colombian town of Armero. The resulting lahars, mudflows moving at roughly 25 miles an hour, poured down river valleys and buried around 85 percent of the town under several metres of mud and rock within hours.

Estimates of the dead range from 23,000 to 25,000; Colombian scientists had warned of the risk weeks earlier, but evacuation orders were delayed. Thirteen-year-old Omayra Sanchez was pinned in the debris for nearly three days before dying; a photograph of her final hours by Frank Fournier won World Press Photo of the Year and became the disaster's defining image.

Beginning on 16 December 1811 and continuing into February 1812, a series of major earthquakes struck near New Madrid in what was then Louisiana Territory, an area with almost no history of large seismic activity. The shaking was strong enough to ring church bells in Boston and was reportedly felt by Andrew Jackson's future troops far to the south.

The quakes temporarily reversed the flow of the Mississippi River and created Reelfoot Lake in Tennessee by dropping land below the water table. Because the region was sparsely settled, the recorded death toll was small, but the sequence remains the strongest known to have struck the eastern half of the United States, and the fault beneath it is still monitored for a repeat.

North Korea's state food distribution system depended on subsidised Soviet and Chinese fuel and fertiliser, and it began failing once that support ended after 1991. Severe floods in 1995 and drought the following year wiped out harvests, and the government was slow to admit the crisis or open its borders to outside aid workers.

Estimates of the dead range from around 240,000, the government's own later figure, to 2 to 3 million from outside demographic studies comparing pre-famine and post-famine census data. The gap reflects how little independent access existed at the time. The period is known in North Korea as the Arduous March, and its scarcity reshaped the country's underground markets for a generation.

A severe windstorm on the night of 31 January 1953 combined with a high spring tide to push a surge of North Sea water against the coasts of the Netherlands, England, Belgium and Scotland. Dykes protecting the low-lying Dutch province of Zeeland gave way in the dark, and many residents drowned in their sleep before any warning reached them.

The Netherlands lost 1,836 people and England 307, with smaller tolls in Belgium and Scotland, for a total above 2,500. The flood exposed how far Dutch flood defences had fallen behind the risk, and it led directly to the Delta Works, the network of dams and barriers the Netherlands built over the following decades.

The earthquake struck at 4:31 a.m. on 17 January 1994, centred under the Northridge neighbourhood of Los Angeles. It measured magnitude 6.7 on a blind fault that had no surface trace, which is why it caught seismologists without a mapped source. Shaking lasted only about 10 to 20 seconds but was among the strongest ever recorded in an urban area of North America.

It killed 57 people and injured over 9,000, collapsing sections of the Santa Monica and Interstate 5 freeways and damaging tens of thousands of buildings. Losses were estimated near 20 billion dollars, and the quake prompted stricter retrofit rules for older concrete and steel-frame buildings across California.

Fire broke out in the attic timbers of Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris on the evening of 15 April 2019, most likely from an electrical fault linked to renovation work underway on the roof. The blaze spread quickly through medieval oak beams that had dried for centuries, and firefighters worked through the night to save the cathedral's twin bell towers.

The 19th-century spire designed by Eugene Viollet-le-Duc collapsed on live television, and most of the wooden roof burned, though the stone vaulting beneath largely held and protected the interior and its relics. Donations for reconstruction reached roughly 850 million euros within days, and the cathedral reopened to the public in December 2024, just over five years after the fire.

Weeks of heavy winter rain in January 1937 pushed the Ohio River more than 20 feet above flood stage along much of its length, from Pittsburgh to Cairo, Illinois. Louisville and Cincinnati were among the hardest hit cities, with large sections left entirely underwater for days.

Around one million people were displaced and roughly 385 died, mostly from drowning, exposure or disease in the flood's aftermath rather than the rising water itself. The scale of the damage pushed Congress to expand the Flood Control Act the following year, funding new dams and levees across the Ohio basin that still stand.

Fire broke out in the reading room of the Centre Block of Canada's Parliament Buildings on the evening of 3 February 1916, likely starting from a cigar left near papers. Members of Parliament were in session at the time and evacuated as the flames spread through the wooden interior.

Seven people died, including the Clerk of the House and three staff who returned for documents. The original 1876 Centre Block, except for its library, burned to the ground; a new building, with the Peace Tower, opened on the site in 1922.

On the night of 13 November 2015, gunmen and suicide bombers attacked a football stadium, several restaurants and the Bataclan concert hall in Paris within the space of about half an hour, working in coordinated teams. The Bataclan attack, where a band was playing to a sold-out crowd, killed 90 people on its own.

130 people died in total and hundreds more were wounded. The Islamic State claimed responsibility, and French investigators traced the plot to a cell that had trained and organised in Syria and Belgium. It was the deadliest attack on French soil since the Second World War.

Famine spread across Persia from 1917 as the First World War drew occupying Russian, British and Ottoman armies through the country, each requisitioning grain and pack animals the harvest depended on. A severe drought that same period compounded the shortage.

Mainstream estimates put the dead at roughly two million from starvation and the disease that followed it, mainly cholera and typhus; the historian Mohammad Gholi Majd has argued for figures as high as eight to ten million, a claim not widely accepted by other scholars. Neutral Persia had no army in the war and no seat at its peace conference.

The magnitude 7.9 earthquake struck off Peru's Pacific coast on 31 May 1970, shaking loose a slab of ice and rock from the north face of Nevado Huascaran, the country's highest peak. The resulting avalanche and debris flow reached speeds estimated near 100 kilometres per hour as it dropped down the mountain.

The town of Yungay, in the avalanche's direct path, was buried almost entirely beneath rock and mud; only a few hundred of its several thousand residents survived, most by reaching a cemetery on higher ground. Counting the earthquake and the landslide together, deaths across the region are put at roughly 47,000 to 70,000, figures assembled from Peruvian government relief records in the disaster's aftermath.

On the night of 8 October 1871, drought-dried forest and slash left by logging crews around Peshtigo, Wisconsin, caught fire and, driven by strong winds, grew into a firestorm that generated its own tornado-like winds and jumped across the Peshtigo River. Many residents survived only by wading into the river itself, though even there some drowned or died of exposure or smoke.

The fire killed at least 1,500 people, and some estimates run higher because the town's own records burned along with it, making it the deadliest wildfire in United States history. It occurred the same night as the Great Chicago Fire farther south, which drew nearly all the era's newspaper coverage, leaving Peshtigo comparatively forgotten despite its far higher death toll.

Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines erupted on 15 June 1991 after weeks of warning tremors that let scientists evacuate tens of thousands of people from the surrounding area, a call credited with keeping the death toll near 850 despite the eruption's scale. Ash and pumice buried farmland and towns across Luzon, and a passing typhoon turned falling ash into heavy, roof-collapsing mud.

The eruption injected around 20 million tonnes of sulphur dioxide into the stratosphere, forming a haze that reflected sunlight and cooled the planet's average surface temperature by roughly 0.5 degrees Celsius for the following year or two. Only Novarupta, which erupted in Alaska in 1912, moved more material in the twentieth century.

A routine pump on the Piper Alpha oil platform in the North Sea was taken offline for maintenance on 6 July 1988, but a night-shift crew, not told the pump's safety valve had been removed, restarted a backup pump that fed straight into the open pipework. The resulting gas leak ignited within minutes, and the fire spread through risers still carrying gas from nearby connected platforms.

167 men died, most from the initial explosions or while trying to reach lifeboats through smoke and flame; 61 survived by jumping into the sea. The Cullen Inquiry that followed found the permit-to-work system had broken down completely and led to a rewrite of North Sea safety regulation, including a requirement for platforms to shut in gas from adjoining fields on command.

An epidemic broke out in Athens in 430 BCE, in the second year of the Peloponnesian War, after the population had crowded inside the city walls under Pericles's strategy of avoiding open battle with Sparta. The historian Thucydides, who caught the disease and survived, described fever, thirst, skin lesions and violent coughing, and recorded that people abandoned the sick and left the dead unburied.

Pericles himself died of it in 429 BCE. Thucydides's description has never been matched conclusively to a known disease, with typhoid, typhus and haemorrhagic fever all proposed, and modern estimates put the dead at up to a quarter of the city's population before the outbreak faded by 426 BCE.

An epidemic swept the Roman Empire from around 249 CE, described by the Carthaginian bishop Cyprian, whose account gives the outbreak its name. He wrote of diarrhoea, vomiting, throat ulcers and fever spreading through Carthage, and treated the suffering as a test of Christian faith rather than purely a medical event.

The disease has never been identified with confidence, with smallpox, measles and viral haemorrhagic fever all proposed from Cyprian's description alone. It recurred in waves for close to two decades, coincided with a period of civil war and economic strain historians call the Crisis of the Third Century, and is thought to have killed the emperor Hostilian in 251 CE.

Bubonic plague reached Constantinople in 541 CE, carried, historians believe, along grain shipping routes from Egypt, and struck the Byzantine capital hard the following year. The historian Procopius, an eyewitness, described bodies piled in the streets and the emperor Justinian himself falling ill and recovering, and the city's dead were eventually thrown into ditches or towers when burial ground ran out.

Ancient DNA recovered from burial sites has since confirmed Yersinia pestis, the bacterium behind later plagues including the Black Death, as the cause. Estimates of the total dead across the Byzantine Empire vary widely, from several million to tens of millions, and the outbreak recurred in waves for roughly two centuries afterward.

Pompeii was a working Roman town of perhaps 12,000 people, with bakeries, brothels, a forum and painted houses, when Vesuvius buried it in 79 CE. Excavations beginning in the eighteenth century found streets, wall paintings and graffiti preserved intact under the ash, giving historians a level of everyday detail almost no other ancient city offers.

Roughly 1,150 bodies have been recovered from the site so far, out of a population most of whom likely escaped during the hours of pumice fall before the deadlier surges arrived. Excavation continues into the twenty first century, and new areas of the town are still being uncovered under continuing volcanic deposits.

The Princess Alice, a paddle steamer returning day-trippers from Kent to London on the evening of 3 September 1878, was struck amidships by the much larger collier Bywell Castle near Tripcock Point on the Thames. The steamer broke in two and sank within minutes, at a stretch of the river where London's sewage outflows had recently been diverted.

More than 650 people died, mostly by drowning in water heavily contaminated by raw sewage, making it the deadliest disaster on an English river. An inquiry found both vessels partly at fault for the collision, and the disaster led directly to new regulations on river navigation lights and rules of the road for shipping on the Thames.

Diana, Princess of Wales, died in the early hours of 31 August 1997 after the car carrying her, her partner Dominic Dodi Fayed and driver Henri Paul crashed in the Pont de l'Alma tunnel in Paris while being pursued by press photographers. Paul, who was found to have been drinking, and Fayed died at the scene; Diana died in hospital hours later. Her bodyguard, Trevor Rees-Jones, was the only survivor.

A French investigation and a later British inquest both concluded the crash was an accident, caused by Paul's driving at speed while impaired, with the paparazzi chase as a contributing factor. Her funeral drew an estimated one million people onto the streets of London, and public grief over her death visibly strained the monarchy's usual reticence.

The earthquake hit the garrison city of Quetta, in what was then British India, before dawn on 31 May 1935. Most of the city's buildings were unreinforced masonry, and the shaking flattened much of Quetta within seconds, trapping residents as they slept.

British authorities placed the army in charge of the response and, to prevent disease from the many unrecovered bodies, sealed off and later demolished much of the old city rather than excavate it fully. Death toll estimates range from about 30,000 to 60,000, a spread that exists because the city was never fully searched before being cleared and rebuilt.

The eight-storey Rana Plaza building near Dhaka collapsed on 24 April 2013, a day after cracks had already appeared in its walls and engineers had told the owner to close it. Garment workers were sent back inside anyway, because factory managers threatened to withhold their pay if they did not report for their shifts.

1,134 people died and more than 2,500 were injured, making it the deadliest garment factory disaster on record. The building had been built without a permit for its upper floors, and it supplied clothing to major Western retailers, prompting a wave of safety agreements across Bangladesh's textile industry afterward.

Drought struck the Volga and Ural regions in 1921 after years of civil war had already stripped peasant farms of grain, horses and labour through requisitioning by both Bolshevik and White forces. The famine that followed affected an estimated 25 to 30 million people across the new Soviet state.

Maxim Gorky's public appeal for foreign aid brought in the American Relief Administration, led by future US president Herbert Hoover, which at its peak fed over ten million people a day. Death toll estimates settle near five million, drawn largely from Soviet demographic reconstructions made years later.

Drought across the Volga basin destroyed the 1891 harvest, and the government's own grain export policy had already thinned the reserves that might have covered the shortfall. Famine and the typhus and cholera that followed it spread through seventeen provinces over the following winter.

Leo Tolstoy organised relief kitchens on his estate and wrote pamphlets pressing the government to act, one of the few instances of a private figure shaping the famine response. Estimates of the dead run from about 375,000 to over 400,000, based on later zemstvo mortality records rather than a wartime census.

Russia's harvests failed for three straight years from 1601, a stretch of cold, wet summers now linked to the same volcanic climate disruption that followed the Peruvian eruption of Huaynaputina in 1600. Grain prices rose several times over, peasants abandoned villages in search of food, and reports describe bark bread and, in the worst accounts, cannibalism in famine-struck districts.

Estimates of the dead run to around two million people, a substantial share of Russia's population at the time, and the famine struck during the political collapse known as the Time of Troubles that followed the end of the Rurik dynasty. Tsar Boris Godunov opened state granaries and capped prices, but the failures outlasted his response and the famine deepened the unrest that followed his death in 1605.

The pandemic later called the Russian flu appeared in Bukhara in the spring of 1889 and reached Saint Petersburg by November, spreading west along railway lines faster than any earlier influenza had travelled. It circled the globe within four months, aided by steamship and rail networks that had not existed during previous pandemics.

Global death estimates run to roughly one million, drawn from mortality records in Europe and North America rather than a single official count. Some virologists have proposed the strain was a coronavirus rather than influenza, based on later serological studies, though this remains disputed. It was the first pandemic tracked in near real time by telegraph.

Samalas, a volcano on the Indonesian island of Lombok, erupted in 1257 with enough force to blow the mountain apart and leave the Segara Anak caldera in its place, roughly six by eight and a half kilometres wide. Old Javanese palm-leaf chronicles, the Babad Lombok, describe the collapse. For centuries afterwards no one connected it to Europe's records of a strange, cold, ash-hazed year.

Ice cores from both Greenland and Antarctica carry the largest sulphate spike of the last 2,300 years at exactly this date, which is how geologists finally traced what had been called the mystery eruption of 1257 back to a specific mountain. The plume is estimated to have reached over 40 kilometres into the stratosphere, cooling the climate worldwide for several years.

An earthquake estimated at magnitude 7.9 struck San Francisco at 5:12 am on 18 April 1906, rupturing the San Andreas fault for roughly 296 miles. The shaking itself lasted under a minute, but ruptured gas lines and collapsed chimneys started fires across the city within hours.

Firefighters, whose chief had been fatally injured in the quake, had few working hydrants after the water mains broke, and the fires burned for three days. Officials at the time reported under 700 dead to protect the city's reputation for investors; modern historians, using cemetery and coroner records, put the toll above 3,000.

SARS was first identified as a distinct illness in southern China's Guangdong province in late 2002, but it reached global attention after a doctor who had treated cases there fell ill in a Hong Kong hotel in February 2003. Guests from that hotel carried the virus onward by air within days, seeding outbreaks in Vietnam, Singapore, Canada and beyond.

The outbreak infected around 8,100 people worldwide and killed roughly 774, a fatality rate near 10 percent that made it far deadlier than seasonal flu even though its total case count stayed small. Aggressive quarantine and contact tracing, coordinated through the World Health Organization, contained it by mid-2003, a response later used as a template when COVID-19 emerged.

The Sewol, a ferry sailing from Incheon to Jeju, capsized off South Korea's southwest coast on 16 April 2014 after a sharp turn shifted its overloaded, poorly secured cargo. The ship had also been illegally modified to carry more passengers and freight than it was designed for, raising its centre of gravity.

304 people died, most of them students from Danwon High School on a class trip. Crew members, including the captain, escaped early while repeatedly telling passengers over the intercom to stay in their cabins. The disaster led to the resignation of South Korea's prime minister and a public reckoning over safety regulation.

On the morning of 23 January 1556 an earthquake near Huaxian in Shaanxi province collapsed hillside cave dwellings and mudbrick towns across a densely settled stretch of central China. It remains the deadliest earthquake on record, and the figure usually quoted, around 830,000 dead, is drawn from Ming dynasty administrative counts of population loss across Shaanxi and neighbouring Shanxi.

Chinese seismologists who have re-examined those records put direct earthquake deaths at closer to 100,000, with the rest of the 830,000 accounted for by famine, disease and displacement in the earthquake's aftermath, or by people who simply migrated away from the ruined region. Either figure describes the same collapse of two provinces at once.

The earthquake struck Sichuan province on 12 May 2008 at magnitude 7.9, its rupture running along the Longmenshan fault beneath mountainous terrain northwest of Chengdu. Landslides blocked roads into the worst-hit valleys for days, and thousands of poorly built schools collapsed during class hours, killing students in numbers that later fuelled public anger at local construction standards.

China's government reported over 69,000 dead and nearly 18,000 missing, with almost 5 million left homeless. Grieving parents who publicly blamed shoddy school construction, a practice critics called tofu-dreg building, faced official pressure to stay quiet, and the earthquake became one of the costliest natural disasters in Chinese history.

The famine followed the collapse of Siad Barre's government in early 1991. Clan militias fought for control of the fertile land between the Jubba and Shebelle rivers, blocking roads and looting food convoys while a drought cut the harvest. Aid could not reach the worst-hit areas of southern Somalia through 1992 because armed groups controlled who ate.

Counts vary because no census existed to check against. Relief agencies and researchers estimated 200,000 to 300,000 deaths, with some studies finding that three in four children under five died in displaced-persons camps around Baidoa and Bardera. The toll drove the UN Security Council to authorise a US-led military intervention, Operation Restore Hope, in December 1992.

A piece of insulating foam broke off Columbia's external fuel tank 82 seconds after launch on 16 January 2003 and struck the leading edge of the left wing, cracking its heat-resistant panels. Engineers reviewed the footage during the sixteen-day mission but concluded, wrongly, that the damage posed no serious risk to re-entry.

On 1 February 2003, superheated gas entered the breach as Columbia descended over Texas, destroying the wing and breaking the shuttle apart at roughly 60,000 metres altitude, killing all seven astronauts aboard. NASA grounded the shuttle fleet for over two years, and the investigation board found the agency's own culture, not just the foam, had allowed known risks to be waved through repeatedly.

The first recognised wave of the influenza pandemic later called the Spanish flu appeared in spring 1918, with early clusters reported at a US Army camp in Kansas before spreading through troop movements late in the First World War. Spain's uncensored press, unlike wartime combatants, reported it openly, which gave the pandemic its misleading name.

That first wave was comparatively mild. It killed far fewer than the second wave that followed by autumn, but it seeded the virus across military bases and ports on several continents within months, ahead of the deadlier resurgence to come.

A second, far deadlier wave of the influenza pandemic swept the world beginning in September 1918, striking healthy young adults especially hard rather than the very old or young typical of most flu seasons. Camp Devens in Massachusetts and cities from Bombay to Cape Town reported overwhelmed hospitals within weeks.

Global death estimates range from roughly 17 million to 50 million or more, a spread this wide because record-keeping in much of Asia and Africa, where the toll was heaviest, was thin or absent. It remains the deadliest single pandemic recorded in modern history.

The St. Francis Dam, built to supply water to Los Angeles, failed just before midnight on 12 March 1928, sending roughly twelve billion gallons down San Francisquito Canyon towards the Pacific. Chief engineer William Mulholland, who had inspected the dam that same morning and pronounced it safe, took responsibility and never worked in public engineering again.

A 1928 claims survey counted 385 confirmed and presumed dead; later researchers, tracing migrant workers and families with no one left to report them missing, put the toll nearer 431. Bodies washed up as far south as the Mexican border for weeks afterward, and some were never identified at all.

Around 6100 BCE, a section of continental shelf off the coast of Norway, in the Storegga area, gave way and slid into the Norwegian Sea. The collapse displaced an enormous volume of water and sent tsunami waves across the North Sea, reaching the coasts of Scotland, the Shetland Islands and the North Sea basin known as Doggerland.

Doggerland was then a low lying plain connecting Britain to continental Europe, still inhabited by Mesolithic hunter gatherer communities. Sediment layers found across Scottish coastal sites and in North Sea cores record the flood, and the event is thought to have hastened the drowning of the last remnants of Doggerland beneath rising post glacial seas.

Over 18 hours on 3 and 4 April 1974, an unusually unstable air mass across the Midwest and South spawned 148 confirmed tornadoes across 13 US states and one Canadian province, the largest outbreak recorded up to that time. Several of the tornadoes were rated F5, the top of the damage scale then in use, including one that tore through Xenia, Ohio.

The outbreak killed 315 people and injured more than 5,000, damage that pushed the US Weather Service to expand tornado watches and warnings and helped justify later investment in Doppler radar coverage across the region. The Xenia tornado alone killed 34 and destroyed roughly half the town's buildings in a few minutes.

Silicon Valley Bank, the main lender to much of the American tech start-up industry, had parked large deposits in long-term government bonds that lost value as interest rates rose through 2022. When it announced a loss on selling some of those bonds on 8 March 2023, depositors, many coordinating over text and social media, tried to withdraw 42 billion dollars in a single day.

Regulators shut the bank down on 10 March 2023 in the second-largest bank failure in US history after Washington Mutual in 2008. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation guaranteed all deposits, even above the usual insured limit, to stop the panic spreading, and two other regional lenders, Signature Bank and First Republic, failed within weeks of it.

A new disease appeared in England within weeks of Henry Tudor's arrival in London after Bosworth in 1485. It began with a sudden sweat, chills and headache and could kill within a day, sometimes within a few hours of the first symptom, which was fast even by the standards of a period used to plague. London alone is thought to have lost around 15,000 people out of a population of roughly 50,000 that summer.

No one has identified the disease with certainty; a hantavirus and a form of influenza are among the modern guesses. It returned in isolated waves over the following decades and Henry VIII feared it enough to postpone a coronation and move his court, but after 1551 it vanished from the English record as suddenly as it had arrived.

The H1N1 strain identified in Mexico in April 2009 was a new mix of swine, bird and human influenza genes, and it spread fast enough that the World Health Organization declared a pandemic within two months, its first such declaration in over forty years. Unlike most flu seasons it hit children and younger adults hardest.

Laboratory-confirmed deaths ran into the thousands, but a 2012 study in The Lancet estimated the true global toll at somewhere between 105,000 and 400,000, because most cases and deaths were never tested or reported. Vaccine supplies arrived late in many countries, and the pandemic was declared over in August 2010.

The earthquake struck at dawn on 20 May 1202, centred in southwestern Syria, and was felt from Sicily to Mesopotamia. Chroniclers of the Ayyubid Sultanate and the Crusader kingdoms recorded widespread destruction across Syria, Lebanon and Palestine, with a tsunami reported along the Syrian and Lebanese coast.

The figure of one million deaths is not the earthquake alone. It combines quake casualties, put by some modern estimates closer to 30,000, with the toll of that year's Nile flood failure in Egypt, which brought famine and epidemic disease across the region. Medieval chroniclers wrote down the larger, combined number without separating the causes.

Mount Tambora, on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa, erupted on 10 April 1815 with a force that blew roughly a third of the mountain away and was heard over 2,000 kilometres distant. Pyroclastic flows and a tsunami killed an estimated 10,000 people directly, and tens of thousands more died in the following months from famine and disease on Sumbawa and neighbouring Lombok.

Ash and sulphur dioxide thrown into the stratosphere circled the globe and lowered average temperatures enough to disrupt harvests on several continents the following year. It remains the largest eruption by volume of any recorded in human history, ranked seven on the Volcanic Explosivity Index, well above Krakatoa or Pinatubo.

The earthquake struck the industrial city of Tangshan, in northern China's Hebei province, at 3:42 am on 28 July 1976, while most residents were asleep in unreinforced brick housing. It measured roughly magnitude 7.6 and gave almost no warning; the city had no seismic monitoring network sensitive enough to have flagged the risk in advance.

China's government did not release any death toll for three years, then announced 242,000 in 1979, a figure still cited as official today. An internal report from weeks after the quake had counted over 263,000 dead nationwide with tens of thousands more listed as missing, and some researchers argue the true toll may exceed 400,000, making the secrecy itself part of the disaster's history.

On 27 March 1977, two Boeing 747s, one operated by KLM and one by Pan Am, were diverted to the small Los Rodeos airport on Tenerife after a bomb threat closed their intended destination, crowding the single runway with aircraft it was not built to hold. Thick fog then reduced visibility on that runway to a few hundred metres.

The KLM captain began his takeoff roll believing he had clearance while the Pan Am jet was still taxiing on the same runway, and the two aircraft collided, killing 583 of the 644 people aboard both planes. It remains aviation's deadliest accident, and the investigation that followed rewrote cockpit procedure worldwide, standardising the phrasing pilots and controllers use to confirm takeoff clearance.

On the morning of 16 April 1947, smoke was spotted rising from the cargo hold of the SS Grandcamp, docked at Texas City carrying over 2,000 tons of ammonium nitrate fertiliser. Crowds gathered on the dock to watch firefighters tackle the blaze, unaware of what the ship held, when it detonated and levelled the harbour district.

The blast killed at least 581 people, including the entire Texas City volunteer fire department, and was powerful enough to be felt 150 miles away and to knock two small aircraft out of the sky. It remains the deadliest industrial accident in US history, and the lawsuits it produced led Congress to pass the Federal Tort Claims Act reforms governing government liability.

In February 2021, unusually far-south Arctic air froze natural gas wellheads and pipelines across Texas just as demand for heating surged. The state's independent power grid, run by ERCOT and not connected to national networks, could not keep up, and operators cut power to millions of homes for days in freezing temperatures.

Texas health officials set the final toll at 246 deaths, mostly from hypothermia, months after the storm. Researchers comparing the period's overall mortality to a normal February concluded the real number was substantially higher, since deaths from untreated medical conditions and carbon monoxide poisoning during the outage were not always recorded as storm-related.

Thalidomide was sold from 1957 as a sedative and, from 1958, marketed specifically to pregnant women for morning sickness, on the strength of animal tests that never checked what it did to a developing foetus. The German company Chemie Grunenthal manufactured it; distributors sold it under dozens of brand names across roughly 46 countries.

Taken in early pregnancy it disrupted limb formation, and an estimated 10,000 to 20,000 children were born with malformations, most commonly shortened or missing arms and legs, before the drug was withdrawn in most markets in 1961 and 1962. The paediatrician Widukind Lenz and the Australian obstetrician William McBride independently traced the pattern to the drug, prompting the withdrawals.

The Aegean island of Thera, now Santorini, erupted around 1600 BCE with enough force to collapse the centre of the island into the sea and bury the Minoan settlement of Akrotiri under metres of pumice and ash. Akrotiri's residents appear to have had warning and fled, since no bodies have been found beneath the debris, unlike at Pompeii centuries later.

The eruption sent ash across the eastern Mediterranean and pumice as far as Egypt and the Levant, and tsunamis likely struck Crete's northern coast. Its precise date is debated: ice cores and tree rings point to the 1600s BCE, while some archaeological pottery links suggest a date decades later, and the gap remains unresolved.

Bubonic plague broke out in Yunnan province in southwestern China in 1855 and spread along trade and river routes, reaching Canton and Hong Kong by the 1890s, from where steamships carried infected rats and fleas to ports across the world. Alexandre Yersin identified the bacterium responsible during the Hong Kong outbreak of 1894, work that finally gave doctors a target rather than a mystery.

Estimates put the global death toll at roughly 12 to 15 million people, with British colonial records crediting India alone with 10 to 12 million deaths and China with about 2.2 million, though record-keeping in rural areas of both countries was uneven. The pandemic is generally dated as running until around 1960, making it by far the longest of the three historically recognised plague pandemics.

A stuck-open relief valve and a misread instrument panel let cooling water drain from Three Mile Island's Unit 2 reactor near Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, on 28 March 1979. Operators, seeing a gauge that misleadingly suggested the core was covered, shut off emergency cooling, and roughly half the reactor's core melted before the mistake was caught.

No one was killed and later health studies found no clear rise in cancer among nearby residents, but the accident emptied a radius of pregnant women and small children on official advice and became the worst commercial nuclear accident in United States history. It froze new American reactor orders for decades and reshaped how control rooms are designed and staffed.

The B-52 was flying a Cold War airborne alert mission over Baffin Bay on 21 January 1968 when a fire broke out in the cabin, forcing the crew to bail out before they could reach the runway at Thule Air Base in Greenland. Six of the seven crew ejected safely; the seventh, who had no ejection seat, died trying to escape.

The bomber crashed onto the sea ice of North Star Bay, where high explosives in its four hydrogen bombs detonated and scattered radioactive material across the ice without triggering a nuclear blast. A four-month cleanup, codenamed Project Crested Ice, removed over 200,000 cubic feet of contaminated ice and debris to the United States, and the secondary stage of one weapon was never recovered.

A warehouse at the Port of Tianjin, storing hazardous chemicals including ammonium nitrate and sodium cyanide far beyond legal limits, caught fire on 12 August 2015 and set off two enormous explosions, one measured at the equivalent of 21 tonnes of TNT. The blast was felt across the city and shattered windows kilometres away.

173 people died, including 104 firefighters who had been sent to fight the blaze without knowing what chemicals were inside. It remains the deadliest single incident for Chinese firefighters since 1949, and the disaster led to criminal charges against port officials for approving storage that violated safety regulations.

RMS Titanic struck an iceberg in the North Atlantic just before midnight on 14 April 1912, and the impact opened a series of gashes along roughly 300 feet of the hull below the waterline. It sank in under three hours, at 2:20 am on 15 April.

Lifeboats had room for barely half the roughly 2,224 people aboard, and several launched only partly filled. About 1,500 died, most from hypothermia in the near-freezing water rather than drowning; the wreck was not located until 1985, more than 12,000 feet below the surface.

Lake Toba in Sumatra sits inside a caldera left by an eruption around 74,000 years ago, one of the largest volcanic events of the last two and a half million years. Ash from it has been traced across the Indian Ocean and as far as eastern Africa, and the eruption is estimated to have cooled the global climate for several years afterward.

Some researchers argued the eruption caused a genetic bottleneck that reduced humanity to a few thousand people. Archaeological sites in India and southern Africa show people living through and after the ash fall with continuous toolmaking traditions, which has left the bottleneck idea increasingly disputed rather than confirmed.

The magnitude 9.0 earthquake off Japan's northeast coast on 11 March 2011 was the strongest ever recorded in the country, and it generated a tsunami that in places reached run-up heights above 30 metres, overwhelming sea walls built for far smaller waves. Whole towns along the Sanriku coast were erased within an hour of the shaking.

Japan's National Police Agency later confirmed nearly 20,000 deaths, with over 2,500 people still listed as missing. Most drowned rather than died from the earthquake itself, and the disaster also disabled the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant, compounding the recovery with a mass evacuation on top of the flood damage.

On the morning of 20 March 1995, five members of the Aum Shinrikyo cult carried plastic bags of liquid sarin onto five Tokyo subway trains converging near government offices in Kasumigaseki. They punctured the bags with sharpened umbrella tips and left the trains, releasing nerve gas into rush-hour carriages and stations.

Thirteen people died and thousands were sickened, some permanently, in an attack the cult's leader Shoko Asahara had ordered to disrupt a police raid he expected. It remains Japan's deadliest act of domestic terrorism, and it prompted a national reassessment of chemical and biological attack preparedness. Asahara was executed in 2018 after years of appeals.

The earthquake struck Tonghai county in Yunnan province, southern China, on 5 January 1970, measuring about magnitude 7.1 and rupturing along a fault that had produced no comparably large quake in living memory. Rural adobe and stone housing across the county collapsed in large numbers within seconds of the first shock.

Chinese authorities did not publish a death toll for years, in keeping with the state secrecy that also delayed reporting on the far larger Tangshan quake six years later; estimates that eventually emerged put the dead at 10,000 to 15,000. The delay meant international earthquake researchers had little reliable data on the event for a generation.

On 18 March 1925 a single tornado tracked roughly 219 miles across Missouri, Illinois and Indiana, staying on the ground for about three and a half hours. Weather Bureau forecasters of the era were forbidden from using the word tornado in public bulletins, for fear of causing panic, so no warning reached the towns in its path.

Six hundred and ninety five people were killed, more than in any other tornado in US recorded history, and roughly 2,000 were injured. Murphysboro, Illinois lost 234 residents, the highest single-town toll on record. The storm's forward speed, near 60 miles per hour at times, outran anyone trying to flee on foot or by car.

A fire broke out on the eighth floor of the Triangle Shirtwaist Company on 25 March 1911, in a Manhattan factory where owners had locked a stairwell door to stop workers taking unauthorised breaks. Many of the 146 dead, mostly young immigrant women, jumped from the ninth floor because the fire escape had collapsed.

The company's owners were tried for manslaughter and acquitted, though a subsequent civil suit paid each victim's family 75 dollars. The fire led directly to new New York State factory safety laws and to Frances Perkins's early career investigating workplace conditions.

Tulip bulbs, newly fashionable in the Dutch Republic after arriving from the Ottoman Empire decades earlier, became a speculative asset traded on contracts rather than the flowers themselves. By early 1637, rare varieties were changing hands for sums that could buy a house in Amsterdam, most of it on credit rather than cash.

The market collapsed within weeks in February 1637 when buyers at a routine bulb auction in Haarlem simply failed to show up, and prices fell by over ninety percent soon after. Modern economic historians dispute how far the mania reached beyond a narrow circle of wealthy speculators, but it is still cited as an early case study in bubbles driven by borrowed money rather than genuine value.

A magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck southern Turkey before dawn on 6 February 2023, followed hours later by a second, magnitude 7.6 quake nearby. Both struck a densely populated region straddling the Turkish-Syrian border, and thousands of buildings, many later found to have been built in violation of safety codes, collapsed with people asleep inside.

Turkish authorities recorded roughly 53,500 deaths and Syrian officials several thousand more, putting the combined toll near 60,000, though aid workers in rebel-held northern Syria said counting stopped before the search did and the true number was likely higher. It ranks among the deadliest earthquakes of the twenty-first century.

TWA Flight 3 left Las Vegas on 16 January 1942 and struck a rock face on Potosi Mountain, Nevada, minutes after takeoff, in clear weather. All 22 people aboard died, including the actress Carole Lombard, who was returning from a war bond rally and had reportedly won a coin toss with her mother to fly rather than take the train.

Investigators found the crew had drifted off course, and a wartime blackout of the usual radio navigation beacon, imposed after Pearl Harbor, is thought to have contributed. Lombard's husband, Clark Gable, later joined the Army Air Forces, and the crash remains the deadliest air disaster in Nevada's history.

Typhoon Haiyan, known locally as Yolanda, made landfall in the central Philippines on 8 November 2013 with sustained winds above 300 kilometres per hour, among the strongest ever measured at landfall. The city of Tacloban took the worst of it: a storm surge several metres high swept inland faster than most residents could evacuate.

The Philippine government's official count settled at just over 6,300 dead, with more than a thousand still listed as missing, though aid workers on the ground argued the true toll was likely higher given how many bodies were never recovered from the surge. Over four million people were displaced across the region.

Mount Unzen had been erupting for two months when, on 21 May 1792, an earthquake shook loose the eastern flank of Mayuyama, a lava dome beside it rather than part of the volcano's own cone. The collapsing slope buried the city of Shimabara beneath it, killing an estimated 10,000 people in the landslide itself before the debris reached the sea.

The mass entering the Ariake Sea threw up a tsunami that struck the opposite shore near Kumamoto, where roughly 5,000 more people drowned, some on the coast Unzen's own debris had not touched. Total deaths are put at about 15,000, still the deadliest volcanic disaster in Japan's recorded history, and the scarred flank of Mayuyama remains visible above Shimabara today.

Engineers had been warned for years that the slope of Monte Toc above the reservoir was unstable, and small slides and tremors through 1963 were treated as manageable rather than as a warning to lower the water. On the night of 9 October, roughly 260 million cubic metres of mountainside slid into the reservoir in under a minute.

The displaced water rose about 250 metres over the dam itself, which held, and poured into the Piave valley below, obliterating the town of Longarone. Counts of the dead range from around 1,900 to over 2,500, since many victims were never recovered from the debris; Italian courts later found the disaster foreseeable and convicted engineers of the dam's builder of manslaughter.

On 22 May 1960 the fault off southern Chile ruptured along roughly 1,000 kilometres of coastline near Valdivia, releasing more energy than any earthquake instruments have measured before or since. Seismologists later rated it magnitude 9.5, a scale that did not exist yet when the shaking happened.

The quake dropped whole stretches of coast by metres and triggered a tsunami that crossed the Pacific, killing people in Hawaii and Japan roughly fifteen and twenty two hours later. Estimates of the dead in Chile itself range from around 1,000 to 6,000, the uncertainty coming from how many victims in remote, sparsely recorded farming districts were ever formally counted.

An earthquake of about magnitude 8.2 struck offshore of Valparaiso, Chile, on 16 August 1906, levelling much of the port city within seconds. Fires that followed, fed by ruptured gas mains, destroyed many of the buildings the shaking had left standing.

Seismological archives list the confirmed toll near 3,800, though newspaper estimates ran as high as 20,000 in the disaster's first confused days. Valparaiso, then Chile's main Pacific port, was largely rebuilt further inland from the waterfront it had occupied before the quake.

The Vasa, a heavily armed Swedish warship built on the order of King Gustavus Adolphus, set out from Stockholm on 10 August 1628 and sailed barely 1,300 metres before a gust of wind caught her. She heeled over, water poured through open gun ports only about 1.2 metres above the waterline, and she sank within minutes in full view of a crowd gathered to watch her leave.

An inquiry followed but assigned no one blame; the ship had been built too tall and narrow, with too little ballast to counter the weight of two gun decks and heavy carved ornamentation, and no one involved was willing to say so to the king. She lay on the harbour floor for over three centuries until she was raised nearly intact in 1961 and is now displayed in Stockholm's Vasa Museum.

Vesuvius erupted on 24 August 79 CE, according to the traditional date drawn from a letter by Pliny the Younger, though some manuscripts and recent archaeological finds point to late October instead. Pliny watched from across the bay and described a cloud shaped like an umbrella pine rising over the mountain before his uncle, Pliny the Elder, sailed toward Pompeii to help and died there.

Pompeii was buried under pumice that fell steadily for hours, giving many residents time to flee, while nearby Herculaneum was hit later by fast moving flows of hot gas and ash that killed people almost instantly. Plaster casts made from the voids left by decomposed bodies in Pompeii's ash preserve the postures of those who did not get out.

A dense atmospheric haze settled over Europe, the Middle East and parts of Asia beginning in 536 CE, dimming the sun for months and, according to contemporaries, for as long as eighteen months. The Byzantine historian Procopius wrote that the sun gave no more light than the moon, and tree ring records from the same years show a sharp drop in growth consistent with severe cold.

The cause was unknown to those living through it, but ice cores now show it followed a major volcanic eruption, likely in Iceland, with a second eruption around 540 CE compounding the cooling. The resulting crop failures and famine across Europe and China are thought to have weakened populations shortly before the Plague of Justinian arrived in 541.

The siege began on 28 February 1993, when ATF agents tried to serve a warrant on the Branch Davidian compound near Waco, Texas, and a gun battle killed four agents and six Davidians. The FBI took over the standoff for 51 days, negotiating with leader David Koresh while surrounding the property with armoured vehicles.

On 19 April, tanks punched holes in the buildings to pump in tear gas, and fires broke out and spread through the wooden structure within minutes. Seventy-six Branch Davidians died, including around 20 children, in a toll established by autopsy and later congressional review. The event became a rallying point for anti-government militia groups through the 1990s.

The White Ship left the Norman port of Barfleur late on 25 November 1120, carrying William Adelin, the only legitimate son of King Henry I of England, along with much of the young royal court. Accounts describe a drunken crew racing to catch up with the king's own fleet in darkness before the ship struck a submerged rock just outside the harbour.

William drowned along with an estimated 300 passengers and crew; only a butcher from Rouen is said to have survived. Henry I had no other legitimate son, and his death set off a succession dispute between Henry's daughter Matilda and his nephew Stephen that erupted into a civil war known as the Anarchy after Henry died in 1135.

The Wilhelm Gustloff left Gdynia on 30 January 1945 crowded far beyond its capacity with German refugees and military personnel fleeing the advancing Red Army, some accounts putting more than 10,000 people aboard a ship built for under 2,000. The Soviet submarine S-13, commanded by Alexander Marinesko, hit it with three torpedoes in the Baltic that evening.

The ship sank within an hour in freezing water, and most of those aboard had no working lifeboats or time to reach them. Because passenger numbers were never properly logged amid the chaos of the evacuation, estimates of the dead range from about 5,000 to over 9,000, making it possibly the largest single loss of life in maritime history.

Sulphate aerosols from Tambora's 1815 eruption spread through the upper atmosphere and reflected enough sunlight to cut global temperatures by roughly half a degree Celsius through 1816. In New England and much of Europe, snow fell in June, frosts killed crops through the summer months, and grain and fodder shortages pushed food prices sharply upward.

Failed harvests in Europe brought famine and typhus outbreaks in regions still recovering from the Napoleonic Wars, and emigration from Vermont and New Hampshire rose as farming families gave up on their land. The unusually dark, cold skies over Switzerland that summer are often credited with keeping Mary Shelley indoors at Lake Geneva while she began writing Frankenstein.

Yellow fever arrived in Philadelphia in July 1793, likely carried by refugees and mosquitoes on ships fleeing revolution in Saint Domingue, and spread through the crowded waterfront district before doctors could identify what was killing their patients. Physicians disagreed sharply on treatment: Benjamin Rush advocated aggressive bloodletting and purging, while others argued rest and fluids saved more lives.

About 5,000 people died before frost killed the mosquitoes in the autumn, out of a population of roughly 50,000, and thousands more fled the city, including much of the federal government, which was then seated there. Philadelphia's Free African Society organised much of the nursing and burial work, a role Rush had urged on the mistaken belief that Black residents were immune to the disease.

Yellowstone has erupted catastrophically three times, and the most recent, around 640,000 years ago, ejected roughly a thousand cubic kilometres of rock and ash and formed the caldera now visible in the park, some 55 kilometres across. Ash from the eruption has been found as far away as the Gulf of Mexico and the Pacific coast.

The caldera did not become a crater in the usual sense: the ground later rose again as fresh magma moved beneath it, and much of the park's present geothermal activity, including its geysers, draws on heat left from that event. No eruption on that scale has happened there since, though smaller lava flows have followed over the intervening millennia.

Around 12,900 years ago, global temperatures that had been rising as the last ice age ended abruptly reversed, plunging much of the Northern Hemisphere back into near-glacial cold within a matter of decades. The cause is debated, with a weakened Atlantic ocean current and a possible comet or meteor impact both proposed, but no single explanation has settled the argument.

The cold spell lasted roughly 1,200 years and disrupted the hunter-gatherer groups who had been living off the retreating ice sheets' resources. Some researchers argue that the resulting scarcity pushed communities in the Fertile Crescent toward deliberately cultivating wild grains, an early step towards the agriculture that spread once the climate warmed again.

Zika virus, spread mainly by Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, had circulated quietly for decades before a large outbreak took hold in Brazil in 2015 and spread across the Americas. Most infections caused mild symptoms or none at all, which let the virus travel widely before doctors noticed anything unusual.

Brazilian doctors then reported a sharp rise in microcephaly, an abnormally small head and underdeveloped brain, among babies born to infected mothers. The World Health Organization declared a public health emergency in February 2016, and the link between Zika infection during pregnancy and birth defects was confirmed later that year.
